title: The essentials for your first account.

title: Know what you are managing
page: The essentials for your first account.
text:
Know what you are managing

OGame is a persistent game: production, timers and fleet movements continue while you are away. Your account is a network of planets and, later, moons. You spend Metal, Crystal and Deuterium on mines, facilities, research, ships and defenses. Energy supports production; it is not a resource you can load into a cargo ship.

Start by finding the selected planet, your resource balances, the event list and the server clock. Open Resources to inspect mines and power, Facilities for supporting buildings, Research for technologies and Fleet for dispatch. Names and positions can differ between desktop and mobile interfaces. Before buying something, open its details and technology prerequisites. A disabled button often means a requirement is missing, not that the page is broken.

Screen or concept | What you use it for | First check
Resources / production settings | Mines, energy and hourly output | Is production fully powered?
Facilities / technology details | Construction, labs, shipyard and unlocks | What is actually blocking my next goal?
Research | Account-wide technologies and prerequisites | What capability does the next level add?
Fleet / event list | Ship missions, timers and returns | Will I be online when valuable ships return?
Galaxy | Positions, nearby players and potential destinations | Am I looking at the intended system and location type?

title: Early production and its constraints
page: The essentials for your first account.
text:
Early production and its constraints

1. A useful mine upgrade needs its resource cost and supporting energy. Solar Plant is a straightforward early source; the energy reference compares the later alternatives.

2. Metal and Crystal support the construction loop. Deuterium becomes important for research, ships and fuel. Preserve resources for the prerequisite that enables the next useful capability.

3. The limiting resource and next unlock matter more than a fixed mine ratio. Include power, storage, transport and the remaining construction time in the comparison.

4. After completion, compare the level, power balance and hourly output under unchanged bonus settings. A nominal production upgrade is not delivering its full benefit if energy or storage blocks it.

A comparison method, not a fixed 10/8/6 build
A fixed mine ratio can be a rough reference, but universe speed, rewards, existing levels and your next unlock change the useful order. The economy guide explains how to compare the actual next level on each mine.

title: Use the technology tree as your map
page: The essentials for your first account.
text:
Use the technology tree as your map

Pick the first capability you need: move resources, explore, settle another planet or progress research. Open that item’s technology details and work backward through the prerequisites. Build only the missing facilities and research levels needed for that near-term goal. A mine makes income; a laboratory or shipyard enables something else. Judge each on the job it performs.

Once you have cargo ships, practise a small transport between suitable owned locations before depending on a large shipment. Confirm the mission, destination type, fuel, payload and return time. Transport does not station the fleet permanently. Read the fleetsaving guide before treating any dispatch as safe storage.

Early rewards and tutorials can accelerate progression. Read what a reward does before claiming or spending it, and do not build a permanent strategy around a temporary event. More stored resources also require a plan to keep them from becoming an easy target.

title: Class, lifeform and play style are different
page: The essentials for your first account.
text:
Class, lifeform and play style are different

Collector, Discoverer and General are account classes with different bonuses. Lifeform species are chosen on planets and unlock their own buildings; Lifeform technologies are another layer again. A miner is a play style, not a requirement to choose one species everywhere. An expedition player still needs mines, cargo, power and fleet safety.

You do not need to settle every advanced choice immediately. Establish production and a reliable routine, then choose the miner, expedition or active-fleet path that fits the time you will actually spend playing. The play-style pages give a investment priorities and explain when to postpone an upgrade.

title: End the session before closing the game
page: The essentials for your first account.
text:
End the session before closing the game

1. Read all active fleet events and queued ship completions. Note what will arrive or finish while you are away.

2. Estimate the unconstrained stock at your next login: current stock plus hourly production multiplied by hours away. Then check when each storage fills, because mine production stops at that limit. Include known deliveries, rewards and queued spending separately.

3. Keep flight fuel and transport capacity available. Do not spend your entire reserve on a last-minute upgrade.

4. Follow the fleetsaving guide for ships and movable resources you cannot afford to lose. Defense is a deterrent, not a substitute for a safe fleet return.

5. Choose a realistic next login and one objective for that visit. A sustainable routine is more valuable than a plan that requires you to watch timers all night.

Check a production change
Compare a mine’s level, hourly output and energy balance before and after a completed upgrade under the same bonus settings. If the actual increase differs from the estimate, inspect energy, storage, production settings and bonus expiry. The economy reference gives worked examples for both upgrades and the next storage deadline.

Name the next constraint

Compare the complete investment

title: Make the offline interval affordable
text:
Make the offline interval affordable

Protect the return, not only the departure

title: What an expedition actually does
text:
What an expedition actually does

Expeditions travel to position 16, hold, resolve a random event and return surviving ships. They need both expedition allowance and a free ordinary fleet slot. Their value depends on the launches you can sustain, not just the size of one find.

Details and worked examples

Build the slot count correctly

title: Discovery and activation
text:
Discovery and activation

For a Human discovery pilot, the Research Centre requires Residential Sector 21 and Biosphere Farm 22. Construct it, support the population and wait for the first slot. Intergalactic Envoys level 1 enables discovery missions from the Galaxy view DNA icons, not position-16 expeditions. Keep it active somewhere before replacing the pilot’s species or slot selection.

A large housing capacity is not the same as actual, sustainably fed population. Higher tiers require conversion buildings; a population shortfall can deactivate research. Stop at the next useful slot rather than funding all eighteen by default.

Discovery limits after transfers: announced change, not a confirmed rollout
Gameforge’s 5 November 2026 announcement, checked 9 November: a transferred or merged account can be blocked from discoveries when its carried-over mission count exceeds the destination server’s age-based limit. Gameforge plans a one-time adjustment of affected counters to the current limit, without removing previous discoveries. It also plans to remove the discovery limit on servers older than one year; servers up to one year old keep their limit. The announced rollout window is November, before Orion’s global release, but this notice does not confirm an exact deployment date. Treat these as pending changes, not rules already active in your universe. After a move, check your discovery counter and the official update before budgeting artefacts or resetting a lifeform tier. A history count higher than the adjusted counter is expected after the fix.

title: Before a large upgrade
text:
Before a large upgrade

- Options in the same slot compete. Record the whole tier before resetting, and check the current warnings and costs. A species switch preserves developed levels for reuse but the replacement setup must support its own active research.

- Test the intended setup on one suitable planet. Compare actual account-bonus changes and keep the ordinary economy, cargo and fleetsave reserve funded.

title: Miner play style
text: Build dependable income with efficient upgrades and a collection routine that fits your life. Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.

title: Choose the routine before the bonuses
text:
Choose the routine before the bonuses

This path fits an account whose income should keep arriving when the player cannot repeatedly launch expeditions or hunt targets. Collector is the natural class to compare for production and crawler support, but choose it against your current bonuses and real activity. A class switch has a cost and can alter logistics. A few excellent expedition days do not prove that a permanently active schedule will suit you.

Passive income still needs collection
Mines do not need relaunching, but storage fills, ships return and resources become targets. The miner routine is less click-intensive, not unattended.

title: Make every existing planet productive
text:
Make every existing planet productive

Use the economy guide’s incremental payback method. Resource weights must be consistent across cost and extra net production. If you value Deuterium differently because of trading or a fuel goal, state that assumption instead of hiding it inside the result.

1. Audit each planet’s next mine level, available energy, storage window and collection route. Fix a production shortage before buying more capacity that cannot run.

2. Compare the next useful mine upgrades across planets. Include supporting energy and the resource that limits your current account goal.

3. Maintain cargo and flight fuel for regular collection. Leave enough capacity to protect your stock between visits.

4. Expand a weak colony in manageable batches. Do not spend all available resources bringing every planet to the same arbitrary level if a smaller plan has better return.

title: Solve the power and crawler system together
text:
Solve the power and crawler system together

Crawlers connect production directly to power demand. Before filling the active crawler limit, check the next batch’s actual energy requirement and net mine gain. If you need additional fusion, include the reactor cost and operating Deuterium. If you need satellites, account for their vulnerability and your ability to rebuild power after a raid.

Read the fusion table before deciding that more Solar Plant levels are always the cheapest option. Higher Energy Technology improves fusion output across the account. At a fixed energy demand it may allow lower reactor utilization and less fuel consumption. Research is an empire-wide purchase; compare its effect across every reactor that will benefit, not just the planet you happen to be viewing.

After any crawler or energy change, compare final total production and net Deuterium with the old setup. The attractive number is the additional income you keep after supplying the power, not only the displayed percentage boost.

title: Develop a production lifeform plan
text:
Develop a production lifeform plan

Rock’tal is a candidate for its mining-focused buildings. Start with one planet, identify the next useful population slot and price the housing, food, tier infrastructure and technology together. Reaching a distant slot is not automatically better than improving an affordable technology you already have.

Choose production, energy or cost-saving technologies for the job you need. The selected species determines local buildings; available Lifeform technologies are not restricted to that species after discovery. Use the Lifeforms guide to compare named options and keep Intergalactic Envoys active where needed for continued discovery.

Spread early, economical research levels where they are affordable rather than chasing one very high local level without comparison. Compare the cost of unlocking another planet’s slot against the gain from a higher level on an established planet. A reset or species switch can interrupt the current setup, so plan it deliberately instead of converting every planet at once.

title: Run one investment queue, not four competing ones
text:
Run one investment queue, not four competing ones

Keep a short queue: one funded improvement, one next target and one optional alternative. Recheck after class changes, new colonies or an expiring bonus. Keep a reserve for transport, energy recovery and fleet safety. A miner with a fragile logistics chain can lose more in one neglected return than a carefully chosen upgrade earns in weeks.

Use one investment shortlist across mines, Plasma, Astrophysics and colony development, crawlers with power, and Lifeform production improvements. Compare their additional net income over the same period and at the same resource values. Research can benefit the whole account; a local upgrade benefits one planet. A temporary resource shortage or a practical collection constraint can reasonably change the order.

Illustrative priority decision
A mine project costs 12 million planning units and adds 300,000 net per day: 40 days. A crawler-plus-power project costs 9 million and adds 300,000: 30 days. The crawler project wins this simple comparison, unless it consumes fuel or Crystal reserved for a more important near-term unlock. Include the same resource weights and supporting costs on both sides.

title: Size storage and cargo for the next absence
text:
Size storage and cargo for the next absence

Calculate the remaining storage window for each resource separately: free storage divided by current net hourly production. Use the shortest window, then leave room for a late login. Imported resources, a completed upgrade or a temporary production item can change the starting balance and rate.

For example, 6,000,000 free Metal storage at 300,000 Metal per hour provides 20 hours before the threshold. A collection after 12 hours adds 3,600,000 Metal and leaves 2,400,000 free space under those assumptions. Crystal and Deuterium need their own checks. This is a storage calculation, not a safe amount to leave exposed.

Cargo should cover the stock you intend to move, with enough fuel and ordinary fleet slots for the route. More storage prevents production from stopping at the threshold; it does not protect the resources from a raid. Compare a storage upgrade with a shorter collection interval, extra transport capacity and a less concentrated holding location.

title: Compare complete projects at the margin
text:
Compare complete projects at the margin

Do not rank entire technologies by their headline bonus. Compare the next affordable purchase with alternatives that solve the same account goal. A short payback is helpful, but a project can still be wrong when it consumes the Crystal or Deuterium needed for a more urgent unlock.

Additive bonus totals also need a marginal calculation. In an illustrative system where output is base × (1 + bonus), moving the bonus from +100% to +110% changes output from 2.00 × base to 2.10 × base, a 5% final increase. Apply this only to a bonus known to share that additive term; do not merge every OGame bonus into one invented bucket.

title: Keep the income running after disruption
text:
Keep the income running after disruption

Separate the next upgrade budget from the operating reserve. The reserve should cover the transport, fuel and power assets your collection routine depends on. A large theoretical daily income is little help if missing cargo leaves it parked on several planets.

After a raid or a class change, recheck power, net Deuterium, active crawlers, cargo capacity and the next collection window before resuming the investment queue. Restore the bottleneck that keeps production usable, rather than rebuilding the previous layout automatically.

Review the plan when your available time changes. A more passive setup may be worthwhile even if a fully active expedition model earns more on paper. Compare realistic weeks, including missed logins, rather than choosing between an ideal miner and an ideal expedition account.

title: Expedition play style
text: Turn a sustainable launch schedule into income, then invest in the bottleneck. Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.

title: Count the launches you will really make
text:
Count the launches you will really make

This path rewards regular attention. Discoverer is the class to compare first for an expedition-centered account, but use the current class bonuses and your universe’s actual rules. Start with the hours you can relaunch, not the hours a spreadsheet assumes you are awake. Record a normal week including workdays and weekends. Mines remain valuable income while you cannot launch.

Do not fund the plan with a lucky screenshot
Resources and useful ship finds vary. Black holes, hostile encounters, empty results and delays are part of the operation. Keep a replacement reserve before expanding it.

title: Build the working fleet and schedule
text:
Build the working fleet and schedule

An expedition build has two different limits: the reward the mechanics allow and the cargo you can bring home. More cargo can solve a transport limit, but excess cargo does not endlessly raise the reward cap. Likewise, travel-speed improvements help only when shorter travel becomes an extra real cycle or a more reliable schedule.

1. Read the expedition mechanics guide. Confirm Astrophysics, total fleet slots, class, economy speed, relevant bonuses and the current reward bracket before calculating a fleet.

2. Create one replaceable expedition fleet with sufficient cargo and the appropriate support ships. Keep your core transport and fleetsave capacity separate.

3. Run a test cycle. Inspect the report and actual returning cargo. Check whether your normal launch time leads to a return you can cover.

4. Repeat only across the slots you can maintain. Save the last batch’s landing window with extra margin for delays before your planned offline time.

title: Grow the bottleneck, not everything at once
text:
Grow the bottleneck, not everything at once

If reports show insufficient carrying capacity, correct cargo before buying another reward bonus. If fleets sit at home after returning, a speed upgrade may do little for daily launches. If you cannot replace a lost working fleet, build the reserve before increasing launch size. If fuel interrupts the routine, fix Deuterium logistics rather than measuring success only in gross loot.

Once the operation is stable, compare slot-unlocking research, cargo capacity and reward bonuses. Price the entire change, including any extra fleet required for a new slot. Astrophysics that adds capacity is not free income if you cannot afford or relaunch the new fleet.

Keep a daily record of launches, resource returns, usable ship finds, fuel and losses. Treat findable ships separately from resources until you have a real use or conversion plan. A resource-weighting method must match your objective; a large Metal-equivalent total can still leave you short of Crystal for research.

title: Choose Lifeforms around the operation
text:
Choose Lifeforms around the operation

Compare the building benefits of Humans, Mecha and Rock’tal against your actual split of expedition and mining income. Do not confuse a planet’s chosen species with the technologies selected into its research slots. Once species are discovered, you can assemble research choices across species while keeping the buildings that fit that planet.

Review Enhanced Sensor Technology, Sixth Sense and Telekinetic Tractor Beam for expedition-focused technology choices. Discoverer Enhancement is relevant when you are actually playing Discoverer. Use the current descriptions and compare the next level’s benefit with the cost to unlock and develop it. The Lifeforms guide explains the population and artefact work needed first.

Cargo or speed selections can be sensible logistics choices, but they displace another technology in the same slot. Estimate the production you give up and ask whether the change increases useful capacity, actual cycles or quality of life. A percentage-point change in an additive bonus is not the same percentage change in your final account income.

title: Rebalance when your routine changes
text:
Rebalance when your routine changes

Review several days or a meaningful batch, not one exceptional result. Change one variable at a time. If work or life reduces your launches, shift investment toward passive production rather than maintaining an old high-attention plan out of habit. The best expedition account is one that you can keep operating without sacrificing fleet safety or sleep.

A useful cargo decision
If a fleet can already carry its permitted maximum find, another cargo upgrade may reduce the number of cargo ships required per launch. That can lower replacement exposure or simplify logistics. It does not by itself prove higher rewards. Measure the benefit you are actually buying.

title: Buy the improvement your reports support
text:
Buy the improvement your reports support

Make one change, preserve its input assumptions and compare a useful batch. A week of results can reveal a recurring logistics problem, but it cannot establish the true frequency of a rare loss. Keep a long-term record without demanding certainty from a small sample.

title: Price a new slot as a complete operation
text:
Price a new slot as a complete operation

A new slot needs more than the research or item that unlocks it. Include the working fleet, any cargo upgrades, fuel stock and enough total mission capacity to keep ordinary transport and fleetsaving available. If the slot is temporary, use only the days when it will actually be active.

Suppose an illustrative permanent-slot project costs 40 million planning units for research and 10 million for its working fleet. If that slot produces an estimated 2 million net per active day, the simple payback is 50 ÷ 2 = 25 active days, not 20. At four active days per week, that is 6.25 weeks before allowing for changing returns or other benefits.

The 2-million figure is an input to test, not an OGame expected return. Estimate it from the extra launches you will really make, with fuel and replacement losses treated consistently. Do not charge the new fleet's entire construction cost against every launch as well as including it in the initial project cost.

title: Value cargo savings and class changes separately
text:
Value cargo savings and class changes separately

A cargo upgrade can be useful even when it does not increase the permitted reward. If the required carrying space is 120 million, ships carrying 40,000 each require 3,000 units. At 50,000 each, they require 2,400. Removing 600 Large Cargos would reduce base replacement exposure by 7.2 million resource units, provided the remaining fleet still meets the useful expedition-point threshold and support requirements.

That is 25% more cargo per ship and 20% fewer cargo ships for the same capacity. It is not a 25% reward increase. Check the actual launch cost before claiming a specific fuel saving, because consumption depends on the ships, drives, speed, route and modifiers.

For a class switch, calculate the entire account: expedition rewards and slots, mining and crawler effects, research time, transport capacity and the schedule. The October Orion notes changed the non-Discoverer comparison on the test server. Avoid importing the older Collector/General expedition multiplier into a current live recommendation without confirming the universe's behavior.

title: Active-fleet play style
text: Choose targets and logistics before accumulating combat hulls. Play-style decisions reviewed 9 November 2026. Compare the current universe, class and active bonuses; examples are conditional planning comparisons.

title: Decide what your fleet is for
text:
Decide what your fleet is for

An active fleet is an operating expense as well as an asset. Decide whether you want small profitable raids, organized alliance combat, debris collection or another specific activity. Those goals require different speed, cargo and fighting capability. General is the class to compare for combat-focused activity, but class bonuses do not turn an unsuitable fleet into a profitable one.

Begin with a role you can evaluate and a fleet you can afford to replace. Do not copy a fixed battleship-to-fighter ratio from an unrelated account. Enemy composition, technologies, defenses, universe settings and allied participation can change the result. A combat simulator is part of planning, not a license to assume a win.

title: Make the support system reliable
text:
Make the support system reliable

1. Learn fleetsaving and practise the route with a small fleet. Know where the main fleet will go when you are offline and how you will cover the return.

2. Prepare enough Deuterium for the intended flight and the next safe move. A successful attack can still strand a fleet if you spend its last fuel.

3. Provide cargo for the intended resource recovery and appropriate recycling capacity when debris collection is part of the plan. Do not count a debris field as recovered profit before it is collected.

4. Use research and facilities to unlock the ships and handling capacity required for the chosen role. Do not fund extra combat hulls while basic fuel and transport are missing.

Defenses cannot protect an unattended valuable fleet
They can change an attacker’s calculation, but a sufficiently valuable target can justify a larger attack. The fleet’s movement and landing plan remain essential.

title: Use a launch decision checklist
text:
Use a launch decision checklist

Read the most relevant intelligence you can obtain. Check what the report actually reveals and what remains unknown. Simulate with the technologies, ships, defenses and universe settings you can support. If a missing input could change the result, run a conservative case or do not take the fight. The simulation is only as reliable as the information entered.

Calculate expected usable loot and collectable debris, then subtract fuel and expected replacement losses in a consistent resource valuation. Allow for the possibility that the target moves, reinforcements arrive or someone else collects debris. Your original expected outcome is not guaranteed because the fleet has launched.

1. Confirm the intended target, mission type, chosen fleet, speed and arrival time.

2. Check that you can monitor the relevant flight and landing window and have a safe post-return plan.

3. Review current rules governing attacks and allied coordination in your universe. Do not infer permission from another server’s settings.

4. After dispatch, verify the event list and continue monitoring for material changes. If the situation no longer matches the plan, reassess rather than treating the original simulation as binding.

title: Support the fleet you actually fly
text:
Support the fleet you actually fly

Read the Lifeform technologies that apply to your chosen ship classes, fuel, speed, cargo or combat characteristics. Compare their benefit with normal combat or engine research and with simply buying the missing support ships. A technology for a ship you rarely use can be poor value despite an impressive percentage.

Mecha is a candidate to examine for fleet-oriented buildings, not a compulsory identity. Planet species, selected research and account class are separate layers. You can preserve an economic building setup while selecting a useful technology from another discovered species. Pilot changes on one suitable planet and record the actual bonus before repeating them across the account.

Research that changes speed can change your usual return schedule. Recheck travel times and fleetsave plans after upgrades. A stronger fleet with a return you cannot cover is not a safer fleet.

Check slot positions before assuming two useful technologies compete. Human Cruiser Mk II is in slot 10 and Mecha General Overhaul (Cruiser) is in slot 9, so a cruiser-focused plan can select both. They still compete with the other choices in their respective slots. Use the current Lifeforms tables for effective contributions and unlock costs instead of treating one ship focus as an automatic empire-wide recommendation.

title: Review the operation, including the miss
text:
Review the operation, including the miss

Keep reports and lessons in an appropriate private place. Public guides do not need real coordinates, fleet schedules, names or account screenshots. Review the sequence: intelligence, decision, launch, monitoring, collection and safe return. Improve the weakest step before increasing the fleet’s value. Alliance cooperation details will live in their own section once its mechanics and operating procedures are confirmed.

A failed raid is still data
If the target moved and the fleet returned empty, record fuel spent, the observation you missed and whether the flight left other commitments exposed. Do not erase the result from the average. A routine with frequent empty flights can be less profitable than a smaller, better-qualified set of targets.

title: Build a fleet for a repeatable job
text:
Build a fleet for a repeatable job

The same ship can be excellent for one job and an expensive passenger in another. Grow the component that prevents a good operation from working: cargo, harvesting, scouting, speed, combat strength or fuel. Do not treat the largest possible fleet value as the objective by itself.

title: Keep operating liquidity after buying hulls
text:
Keep operating liquidity after buying hulls

Reserve Deuterium for the planned operation and the next safe move. Use the dispatch screen with the real composition, route and speed. Fuel reductions, class modifiers and server settings should be reflected in that number; do not subtract a remembered percentage again.

If a moon holds 1,000,000 Deuterium, a planned attack needs 600,000 and a safe post-return departure needs 500,000, the combined plan is 100,000 short. Expected loot is not a reliable substitute for fuel already in the right place. Replenish the moon or change the operation before committing.

Keep replacement and transport resources available as well. A win that leaves the account unable to move its other fleets can be a poor overall decision. Recycle only what you can actually collect, and do not spend predicted debris before the harvest result exists.

title: Test the decision when the target changes
text:
Test the decision when the target changes

Use at least a normal case and an adverse case. The adverse case should reflect the uncertainty that matters: missing combat research, extra defenders, less loot, incomplete debris recovery or a changed arrival. A simulated victory with one optimistic input is not enough for an expensive launch.

If full debris recovery produces 4 million net but no recovery produces zero, the operation depends on harvesting. Treat recycling capacity and timing as a requirement, not a later convenience. If the target can move the loot and the remaining operation loses resources, decide in advance what evidence would make you recall while recall is still available.

Review empty flights and abandoned plans alongside successful hits. Useful metrics include net resources per supervised hour, fuel spent on misses, permanent ship losses and whether every return was handled safely. These are management choices, not reasons to publish sensitive coordinates or flight schedules.

page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text: What to build first when Orion is enabled, how to spread IAS levels across planets, and what observed mission cards show about possible rewards at higher levels. Orion preparation reviewed 9 November 2026. Reward examples are selected PTS beta18 mission cards from 28 October 2026, not current live quotes or collected income. Confirm activation and prices in your universe.

title: Confirm the feature before spending
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
Confirm the feature before spending

The source review of 9 November 2026 recorded Mars and Nembus as US merge targets for the 9–12 November window. That announcement does not explicitly confirm their Orion activation flag. A universe being newly created or receiving merged accounts does not by itself establish that Orion is enabled. Check the feature in your universe before committing resources.

The official version 13.1.0 notice limits its 6 November Orion activation to universes launching that day. Gameforge’s launch release says a global rollout is planned for 30 November. Neither statement settles the merge targets individually. Open your universe’s technology tree and check that the IAS, Lithium conversion and anomaly interface are available before committing a build budget.

Use this guide when Orion is enabled
The sequence below is a conditional Orion plan, not a claim that a named target is already active. The live technology tree supplies the exact prerequisites, fields, construction prices and restrictions. A missing feature is a reason to wait, not to rebuild around an assumed release date.

title: What to build first, and why
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
What to build first, and why

Keep your mines, energy and fleet-safety routine working. Orion adds another use for resources and attention; it does not replace the economy that pays for it. This is a spending order, not a fixed timetable or a requirement to use Dark Matter.

1. Check the live prerequisites and spare fields on each planet you can practically supply. Build the minimum prerequisite facilities needed to place an IAS there. Do not add expensive facilities solely because an old PTS screenshot had them.

2. Place IAS level 1 buildings across those usable planets. For a target total, buy the cheapest next scanner level available, rather than pushing one planet far ahead. Equal per-planet exponential prices make a balanced network the least-resource route to that total.

3. Aim first for a modest total such as IAS 50, then stop to run the loop. Enable a small, affordable Lithium conversion workload and read both the hourly input and output. Check the current storage limit; leave a reserve for claiming the reward as well as finding the mission.

4. Scan for a manageable mission, inspect its actual level, type, stars, waves, participation rules, duration, requirements and reward claim cost. Use ships or delivery cargo you can afford to commit, and cover the return. A large possible reward is not a completed or claimed reward. Check the claim deadline and actual reward-delivery destination; do not assume the reward can wait until your next login.

5. Complete the qualifying mission and confirm the Control Center unlock. Buy a low level of a relevant bonus building only after its effect and price make sense for the missions you actually run. A ship-focused building has little immediate value if you keep choosing resource rewards.

6. Advance through the next useful checkpoints: 100, 150, 200, 250, 300 and 350 total IAS. Recheck affordable missions, Lithium supply and claim costs at each step. Continue beyond a checkpoint only when it supports a mission or bonus you can use.

7. Buy extra discovery capacity, scan results or deeper bonus-building levels only when the existing limit is regularly stopping profitable play. More slots are not more income if you cannot fund claims or finish missions.

Balanced levels optimize access, not everything
The cheapest network for a given total IAS is not automatically the best Lithium-throughput layout. Local scanner levels, conversion workload, input availability and current bonuses also matter. First solve the access target; then measure the bottleneck before specializing a planet.

title: Total IAS is the sum across your planets
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
Total IAS is the sum across your planets

Use T = L1 + L2 + … + Ln, where each L is one eligible planet’s IAS level. Total IAS supports the selectable anomaly level. It is not the exact level of every result, a reward multiplier by itself, or a building level on one planet. Read the mission card and the live unlock requirement.

For a balanced plan from level zero across n planets, set q = floor(T / n) and r = T − n × q. Build r planets to q + 1 and the other n − r to q. Existing uneven accounts should compare the next available upgrade prices instead of demolishing anything to match an illustration.

The table uses 15 hypothetical, equally priced and usable planets. It is not an account requirement. Amounts are cumulative construction costs from IAS 0, in units of each named resource, calculated with the preserved beta13 cost model. They are not current live quotes and do not include prerequisites.

Why distribute the levels?
In the same historical model, total IAS 350 across 15 planets costs 32,992,180 Metal. Across 10 planets at level 35 each, it costs 2,446,262,300 Metal. The total access level is the same; the second plan buys much deeper, more expensive local levels. This comparison isolates construction cost. It does not say the two layouts have equal Lithium output or equal real-world setup costs.

350 is a progression milestone, not a universal first purchase
The historical guide used 350 to reach the final recorded building unlock. That does not prove rushing there has the best payback. A smaller account can stop earlier while it learns mission costs; an established account can advance faster if it can fund and complete the missions. title: Map total IAS to a scan setting and a mission range
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
Map total IAS to a scan setting and a mission range

Keep three numbers separate: T is total IAS across your planets; S is the anomaly level selected for a scan; M is the level of the discovered mission. Total IAS sets the maximum selectable level, but you can choose a lower scan level. The documented variation of about ±20% is around the selected level S. It maps mission access, not the size of the reward.

Before any undocumented integer rounding, the working range is approximately 0.8 × S ≤ M ≤ 1.2 × S. At the maximum setting, S = T, so this becomes approximately 0.8 × T to 1.2 × T. If you select a lower level, use that selected value instead of your total IAS. The examples below explicitly assume a maximum-level scan; decimal endpoints are arithmetic, not a claim about the game’s rounding rules.

The reported IAS-693 example fits the level range
At a maximum-level scan with total IAS 693, the arithmetic range is about 554.4–831.6. The observed mission level 658 lies inside it and is about 5.05% below 693. The mission’s selected scan setting was not visible, so maximum-level scanning is an explicit assumption here, not an observed fact.

Do not reverse the percentage the wrong way
From a mission level M alone, divide: S is approximately between M / 1.2 and M / 0.8, before unknown game rounding. For M = 658, that is about 548.33–822.5. Applying ±20% directly to 658 gives the wrong inverse. This only brackets total IAS if the scan used the maximum setting S = T; otherwise the total IAS can be higher. Do not infer an exact account total from a mission card. For the separately reported total IAS 693, also require S ≤ 693, narrowing the compatible selected-level interval to about 548.33–693. That still does not identify which setting was used.

Observed possible rewards can exceed one billion per mission

The evidence pairs a reported total IAS of 693 with a card-visible level-658 Alien Encounter in PTS beta18. That card displayed approximately 1.415 billion Metal + Crystal + Deuterium in possible rewards for one mission. This supports billion-scale possible rewards at that reported IAS; it does not establish a typical payout or a reward formula.

The screenshots establish actual mission levels, templates, stars, waves and displayed reward costs. Total IAS 693 is separately reported for the level-658 example only, not visible on its mission card. The other four IAS totals and every selected scan level remain unknown. Every resource amount was marked approximate in the interface, so the sums below are approximate too.

Raw resource units means the arithmetic sum of Metal + Crystal + Deuterium. It is not Metal-equivalent value: one unit of each is simply counted as one. Ships and other non-resource rewards are excluded from this sum. The displayed Reward Costs are shown separately in Lithium units. These rounded interface amounts were not paid or independently verified as the full liability; scan costs, conversion inputs, fuel, delivery costs and losses are not deducted.

For planning at a different IAS total, first map the mission-level range from the scan setting, then compare current cards of the same template, stars, waves and mode. These five unlike cards support a scale comparison, not a line to extrapolate to IAS 500 or 1,000. More IAS opens higher mission levels; it does not assign one payout to every mission in that range.

title: Turn possible rewards into a measured return
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
Turn possible rewards into a measured return

1. Record the game version, total IAS, selected scan level and actual mission level separately. Keep the mission type, stars, mode, waves, class, bonuses, participation and claim fraction alongside each result. Compare like with like.

2. Record the total actually claimed across the mission, not one wave copied as a whole-mission total or the possible reward shown before completion. Treat an unknown value as unknown.

3. For a given IAS band, divide the total actual reward by all attempted comparable missions if you want a return that includes failed attempts. Keep reward per successful full claim as a separate measure. Several observations are more informative than one lucky card.

4. Observe a full real day or week, including waiting for Lithium, travel and attention. The simplest gross daily return is total actually claimed over that period divided by elapsed days. Keep denominators matched: average per attempt × attempts per day, or average per successful full claim × successful full claims per day. Never multiply an average that already includes failures by successful completions only.

5. Subtract the resources spent producing the Lithium for scans and claims, plus delivery costs, fuel and unrecovered fleet losses. Use a stated exchange rate if combining Metal, Crystal and Deuterium into one value. Do not treat Lithium as free because it is produced in a building.

6. Compare the measured extra daily net return with the price of the next IAS upgrades. A rough payback is upgrade cost divided by extra daily net return, in the same value units. If the extra return is zero or negative, that calculation gives no positive payback.

A large card is an opportunity, not income already earned
The observed level-658 card offered ≈1.415 billion raw resource units, but its collected-reward area was still empty. Keep that possible amount separate from the amount actually claimed and from the resources needed for its displayed 55.418 million Lithium reward cost, subject to confirmation when claiming. Value Metal, Crystal and Deuterium with an explicit exchange rate before comparing net returns. No daily-income figure can be inferred from this card alone.

title: Patch changes that an old Orion guide can miss
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:

title: What the preserved cost model calculates
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
What the preserved cost model calculates

For the historical IAS model, the base resource costs are 84 Metal, 42 Crystal and 14 Deuterium. At target level L, the formula is floor(Base × 1.5^(L − 1)) separately for each resource. A current-to-target result sums each next level through the target. The implementation uses exact integer arithmetic with 3/2, not floating-point estimates.

The beta13 official notes increased the scaling factor from 1.4 to 1.5. The preserved calculator follows 1.5, represented exactly as 3/2. Its outputs remain historical projections and require a live-price check before use.

This calculator prices one planet only. A combined account target of 350 means adding the scanner levels on all eligible planets; do not type 350 into a single-planet target field. For a network, calculate each planet separately and add the same resource columns. Prices exclude prerequisites, facilities, transport and opportunity cost.

Worked historical example: IAS 0 → 2
Level 1: 84 Metal + 42 Crystal + 14 Deuterium.
Level 2: 126 Metal + 63 Crystal + 21 Deuterium.
Combined projection: 210 Metal + 105 Crystal + 35 Deuterium.
This verifies the calculation method, not today’s in-game pricing.

title: A final check before the next build
page: Start Orion with a plan for your whole account.
text:
A final check before the next build

1. Confirm Orion activation, current prerequisites, construction prices and your usable planets in the current universe.

2. Keep total IAS, each local IAS level, actual mission level and completed-mission unlocks separate.

3. Compare one live construction price against the historical model before using its network table or calculator. A mismatch means stop relying on that projection.

4. Reserve enough Lithium for the scan and the reward claim, and price the ordinary resources used to make it.

5. Use actual claimed rewards and sustainable completion rates to decide on the next checkpoint. Keep private coordinates, planet names, balances, fleet details and screenshots out of public research.

title: Lifeform population and unlock builds.

title: What these builds measure
text:
What these builds measure

These cost-oriented reference endpoints unlock useful research milestones under the stated equilibrium model. They are not universal optimal builds, a cheapest chronological purchase order, or an instruction to demolish higher levels. Retain existing higher levels and meet all prerequisites. The next useful research slot is usually a better target than all eighteen at once.

All Lifeform buildings use zero ordinary planet fields. There is no ordinary-field advantage between these population packages. Least total resources, least weighted resources, fewest upgrades and fastest completion are different goals. Queue speed, growth time, existing buildings and items can change the best next purchase.

The examples assume no population item or research modifier. Species experience boosts technology bonuses, not these population-building effects. Do not add the old Trader population bonus: it was a bug removed in 2023. Species choice is mainly about local building benefits; researched technologies from discovered species can be selected independently.

Capacity, sustainable population and actual population differ
Housing is a ceiling. Food determines how much population can be supported indefinitely, while the current counter must still grow to that level. Stored food can bridge a shortage but is not permanent food production. These endpoints deliberately feed slightly less than full housing capacity while still meeting the target. T2 and T3 are chained tier proportions; do not add all tier counters and subtract that sum from housing.

title: Reproduce the population model
text:
Reproduce the population model

Let q = housing level, f = food-building level, s = T2 conversion-building level and t = T3 conversion-building level. H = base housing × housing factor^q × (q + 1) × housing multiplier. C = base consumption × 1.15^q × (q + 1) × consumption multiplier. F = base food × food factor^f × (f + 1) × food multiplier.

Sustainable T1 = H × min(1, F/C). T2 = sustainable T1 × s/100. T3 = T2 × t/100. Compare the appropriate tier with its adjusted slot requirement. Use unrounded values internally; displayed counters are approximate because game rounding can differ. C and F are common-scale model values for the food ratio, not a claim about live hourly display units.

- Humans: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.015 × Skyscraper; consumption multiplier = 1 − min(0.80, 0.01 × Food Silo); food multiplier = 1 + 0.05 × Biotech Lab.

- Rock’tal: these population-package multipliers are all 1. Megalith and Mineral Research Centre affect building costs, not this food/housing ratio.

- Mechas: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Production Assembly Hall; food multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Microchip Assembly Line; consumption multiplier = 1.

- Kaelesh: housing multiplier = 1 + 0.02 × Chrysalis Accelerator; consumption multiplier = 1 − min(0.50, 0.01 × Antimatter Convector); food multiplier = 1.

title: Growth, timing and activation
text:
Growth, timing and activation

Finished buildings do not instantly activate a slot. The actual tier counter must reach the requirement and remain there. Official version 9.0.3 made population growth independent of server speed, so an ×8 economy does not imply ×8 population growth. A complete current growth-ETA formula has not been independently verified here.

Human Food Silo reduces upkeep while Skyscraper and Biotech Lab support housing and food. Mechas combine housing and food boosters. Kaelesh combines housing, upkeep and requirement reductions; Cloning Laboratory can be a growth-time option but is not needed for the shown equilibrium endpoint. Rock’tal instead gains cost-reduction options whose purchase timing matters.

title: Unlock tiers without buying unnecessary population
text:
Unlock tiers without buying unnecessary population

There are eighteen research slots arranged in three tiers. Housing and food support the population; conversion buildings make higher-tier population available. For Humans, Academy of Sciences converts toward tier 2 and Neuro-Calibration Centre toward tier 3. For Rock’tal, the analogous progression uses Rune Forge and Oriktorium. Inspect the population tier required by your target slot: a large tier-1 population does not automatically satisfy a tier-2 requirement.

1. Pick the next useful research slot and write down its displayed population requirement and tier.

2. Price the missing housing, food, research-building prerequisites and conversion levels as one package.

3. Build food and housing support, then the required conversion infrastructure. Check actual tier counters rather than total population alone.

4. Wait for stable population and confirm that the research stays active. A population shortfall can deactivate unlocked technologies.

5. Buy a useful research level and compare the actual gain before pursuing the next population threshold. Do not rush tier 3 simply because a template shows all eighteen slots.

title: Develop the species buildings in phases
text:
Develop the species buildings in phases

For a mining-oriented Rock’tal pilot, first use Meditation Enclave, Crystal Farm and Rune Technologium to reach the useful early research slots. Then price Magma Forge for metal, Crystal Refinery for crystal and the lifeform Deuterium Synthesiser for deuterium against another ordinary mine level. The lifeform synthesiser is a different building from the normal resource-menu synthesizer.

Before a large development phase, compare the cost savings from Megalith with the cost of buying it. Develop Rune Forge only when a useful tier-2 slot justifies the extra population infrastructure; use the same test for Oriktorium and tier 3. Add Disruption Chamber when the energy benefit or reduced demand solves a measured constraint. This gives a sequence with stop points rather than an unfunded all-buildings shopping list.

An expedition-focused player can still use Rock’tal buildings while selecting expedition technologies discovered from another species. Humans and Mecha deserve comparison when their research-amplifying buildings fit a developed, active account. Species, player class and research selection are not required to match names.

title: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text: How to read the research tables, combine eligible bonuses and distinguish caps from current-version uncertainties. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Source-model reference, not a live-account measurement. Official workbook vintage and current implementation caveats are stated below; live Techinfo takes precedence.

title: Base effects and eligible targets
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Base effects and eligible targets

Every research effect in the four tables contributes account-wide, but only to its named target. Selection and levels are local to each planet. The planet’s inhabiting species is independent of the technology’s origin; the same unlocked technology can be selected on multiple planets. Slots 1–6 are T1.1–T1.6, slots 7–12 are T2.1–T2.6, and slots 13–18 are T3.1–T3.6.

The ship-stat package means structural integrity, shields, attack, cargo capacity and base speed. It does not include fuel consumption. Civilian ships here means Small Cargo, Large Cargo, Colony Ship, Recycler and Espionage Probe, not Pathfinder. Probe cargo still depends on universe settings.

Production percentages act on the relevant production basis, not necessarily on an already-bonused total. Flight-speed, ship-stat and expedition coefficients are not complete final-speed, flight-time or yield equations. Read a research name together with its target: Low-Temperature Drives affects Espionage research, and Rune Shields affects Armour research.

title: How contributions stack
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
How contributions stack

For an ordinary linear effect, the per-planet contribution is base coefficient × research level × (1 + inhabiting-species experience bonus + applicable building bonuses). Add eligible contributions across planets, then apply the relevant effect-category cap. Bonuses inside this multiplier are added, not multiplied independently. The Cloning Lab’s technology amplification applies to Kaelesh technologies.

This expression describes the Lifeform contribution, not the complete final mine, ship, flight or reward calculation. Do not amplify an already-final in-game bonus a second time. Special handling, such as the first level of Intergalactic Envoys, can differ from the ordinary expression.

A coefficient is not the final production change
High-Performance Extractors gives 0.06% per level. At level 10 its base contribution is 0.6%; with a combined 10% applicable amplifier it becomes 0.66%, not 10.6%. Two such eligible planets contribute 1.32 percentage points to the relevant production modifier before other system rules.

title: Caps and version limits
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Caps and version limits

These are effect-category caps in the referenced definitions, not a separate allowance for every technology. “No cap specified” is not proof that every downstream system is unlimited.

Fuel: older Lifeform cap versus later global cap
Efficiency Module and Heat Recovery each have a verified base reduction of 0.03% per level. The 2023 workbook and pinned Tracker Lifeform definitions retain a 30% Lifeform cap. The official live version 13.0.0-r8 notice of 29 July 2026 instead states a 90% global fuel-reduction limit. The exact current Lifeform/class/global combination was not independently verified. Do not claim all fuel reduction is capped at 30%, or that each technology independently allows 90%. Check current dispatch fuel and Techinfo.

Effect category | Reference limit | Interpretation
Targeted research/building resource cost | 50% reduction | Applies only to the named target; do not treat time reduction as resource savings.
Targeted research/building time | 99% reduction | Combine eligible reductions within the applicable calculation.
Crawler energy use | 50% reduction | Ion Crystal Modules does not raise the overload setting.
Fuel refunded on recall | 90% refund | Slingshot Autopilot refunds fuel on recall; it is not a general flight-fuel reduction.
Complete-fleet-loss expedition event probability | 50% relative reduction | Psionic Network targets this event probability, not all expedition losses or combat damage.
Raw resource/energy production, ship/defense stats, cargo, phalanx range and class amplification | No cap specified in these definitions | Final-system limits and integer rounding can still matter.
Ordinary flight-fuel reduction | Version conflict: older LF definition 30%; later global limit 90% | See the fuel caveat below; do not substitute either number for an unverified combined formula.

title: Class enhancements
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Class enhancements

Rock’tal Collector Enhancement, Mechan General Enhancement and Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement all occupy slot 18 / T3.6. Each has a base +0.2% per research level to eligible bonuses of the corresponding active class. They do not give an account another class.

A total 50% enhancement means an eligible base perk ×1.5, not an extra 50 percentage points added to every perk. Integer perks have rounding thresholds. The official October 2026 expedition guide gives one extra expedition slot per 50% Discoverer enhancement, amplifying the class’s base +2 slots.

Class enhancement | Excluded perks
Rock’tal Collector Enhancement | Crawler overload ability/setting; building-acceleration discount.
Mechan General Enhancement | Light Fighter instant Deathstar destruction chance; transport of attacking wreckage to the starting planet; detailed fleet-speed controls; shipyard-acceleration discounts.
Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement | Expedition-debris visibility; inactive-player loot; research-acceleration discounts.

title: Effects that need an extra check
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Effects that need an extra check

- Intergalactic Envoys unlocks discovery missions at level 1. The official workbook lists a nominal +1% discovery-flight speed per research level; pinned Tracker gives zero speed bonus at level 1, then 1% × level at higher levels. Exact first-level handling and live travel time were not independently verified. It does not improve discovery or artefact odds.

- Telekinetic Tractor Beam, Enhanced Sensor Technology, Sixth Sense and Gravitation Sensors increase the quantity of their named expedition find, not the chance of that event. Telekinetic Drive affects expedition travel speed, not holding time.

- Psionic Network reduces the probability of the complete-fleet-loss expedition event relatively. It does not reduce pirate/alien battle damage, remove every risk or make fleetsaving on expeditions safe.

- Ion Crystal Modules has +0.1% crawler production efficiency and −0.1% crawler energy use per level in the checked definitions. The exact enhanced crawler-production equation remains unverified because the pinned Tracker implementation is internally inconsistent. No final output equation or higher overload setting is inferred.

title: Plan the tier before spending artefacts
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Plan the tier before spending artefacts

Artefacts let you select a desired technology rather than rely on a random choice. The official information describes different costs by tier. Before spending, write out your desired selections for the whole tier and compare the total with your inventory. The FAQ warns that changing selections can involve resetting the tier and selecting its technologies again.

The published artefact prices are 200 for a tier-1 selection, 400 for tier 2 and 600 for tier 3. Four deliberate tier-1 selections therefore need 800 artefacts; that is selection currency, not the resources needed to research the chosen technologies. Record the other selections before resetting, because they may also need to be selected again.

Treat a reset as a small migration project: record current selections, check the current interface warnings and costs, and know the desired end state. Do not reset while tired simply because one technology looks better. If a species switch is also involved, evaluate the new building setup and population unlocks before expecting the old bonus to remain active.

Illustrative comparison
Imagine one new research level produces an estimated 20,000 additional resources per day across your account and costs 400,000. Its simple payback is 20 days. A second option appears cheaper at 150,000 but requires 500,000 of population infrastructure first: compare 650,000 with its benefit. These figures illustrate total-cost reasoning, not real technology costs.

title: Choose a build strategy for your actual income
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Choose a build strategy for your actual income

These are candidate paths, not an instruction to choose every listed technology. Options in the same slot compete with one another. Preview the slot’s four candidates and their current descriptions before committing artefacts.

Account pattern | Early research candidates | Later direction and decision rule
Passive miner | High-Performance Extractors: all-resource production; Acoustic Scanning: crystal; High Energy Pump Systems: deuterium | Compare income gained per full upgrade cost. Consider Rock’tal production buildings and Collector Enhancement if Collector is active.
Regular expeditions | Telekinetic Tractor Beam: ship finds; Enhanced Sensor Technology: resource finds | Add Sixth Sense for resource finds and consider Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement for an active Discoverer. Value these using actual launches, not an imagined maximum.
Active fleet | Plasma Drive: speed except Deathstars; Efficiency Module: flight fuel reduction | Choose a ship-specific General Overhaul only for ships you use, such as Battlecruisers. Simulate the fleet after updating bonuses.
Logistics-limited account | Cargo Hold Expansion: civilian cargo capacity | Compare fewer ships or trips against the production or expedition technology sacrificed in the same slot. More cargo does not by itself raise the expedition reward cap.

title: Pilot the plan, then roll it out
page: Lifeform research: stacking, caps and selections.
text:
Pilot the plan, then roll it out

Try the intended setup on one suitable planet before repeating it everywhere. Record the cost to reach the slot, the research cost and the actual bonus change. If you cannot explain where the improvement appears, investigate before scaling. A copied template may depend on a different class, income mix or activity level.

Compare another level on a mature planet with an early level on a less-developed planet, including prerequisites. Keep core economy, cargo and fleetsave reserves funded. Revisit the plan when your play pattern changes: an expedition-heavy setup deserves a new review if you stop launching regularly. Your account should support the game you actually play, not a schedule you no longer keep.

A species switch preserves previously developed levels for later reuse, but the new species must support and unlock its own selected research. Expect a transition, not an instant replacement of every bonus. Before changing a working setup, record selections, population and account totals. Compare the gain using the production breakdown: a one-percentage-point bonus is not necessarily one percent of an already-bonused total.

title: Compare economic investments.
text: Mine costs, incremental output, resource bottlenecks and the storage you will actually use. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.

title: Know what each mine does
text:
Know what each mine does

Metal funds much of your construction and fleet growth. Crystal is often the limiting material for research and advanced infrastructure. Deuterium is both a construction/research resource and the fuel for operations. Mines provide recurring income while you are offline, but only within energy and storage constraints. An upgrade raises future production; it does not immediately deliver a lump sum of resources.

The standard mine-output terms at full power and ×1 economy are 30 × L × 1.1^L for metal, 20 × L × 1.1^L for crystal, and 10 × L × 1.1^L × (1.44 − 0.004 × Tmax) for deuterium. Tmax is the planet’s maximum temperature. These terms exclude natural base income, slot bonuses, class, Plasma Technology, lifeforms and other modifiers. Multiply resource production by economy speed, then account for your actual bonuses. Do not multiply the power requirement by economy speed.

These are calculated baseline values
The table shows formula terms rounded to two decimals, not a promise of the total shown in your resource screen. Compare the screen’s base mine row and modifier rows separately.

Example at mine level 10 | Unmodified mine output/hour | Why it matters
Metal Mine | 778.12 metal | Construction material; slot bonuses can change the comparison
Crystal Mine | 518.75 crystal | Research needs can justify prioritizing it despite lower volume
Deuterium Synthesizer, Tmax +40°C | 332.00 deuterium | Temperature-dependent fuel production
Deuterium Synthesizer, Tmax −90°C | 466.87 deuterium | Same level, more output because the planet is colder

title: Early production and infrastructure
text:
Early production and infrastructure

1. Open Resources and inspect the Metal Mine, Crystal Mine, Deuterium Synthesizer and Solar Plant. Read the next-level cost, completion time and energy demand.

2. Use the Solar Plant to support the next mine increase. Check the energy balance after completion; persistent shortages mean the mine is not delivering its intended full output.

3. Build metal and crystal capacity toward a named early unlock. If crystal is delaying that unlock, increase crystal rather than following a fixed metal-to-crystal level ratio.

4. Develop deuterium before research and ship fuel become the bottleneck. Do not drain all fuel into a queue once you have ships to move.

5. Open Facilities for Robotics Factory, Shipyard and Research Lab only as the next unlock requires them. Use the technology tree to see the missing levels.

6. Before your break, check when each resource will fill storage. Spend on the planned upgrade, improve storage when justified, and establish cargo logistics as ships become available. Return to Resources to verify the result.

title: Measure before you spend
text:
Measure before you spend

Start on one planet. Write down hourly metal, crystal and deuterium output, available energy, storage space and free fields. Record your class and the universe economy speed next to those numbers. Use the values actually displayed, including active bonuses. A guide written for a different universe cannot supply your production forecast. Refresh the screen after a queue finishes before comparing the result.

Mines need energy, storage limits production, and facilities provide infrastructure rather than direct mine output. These are different problems. An energy shortage is not fixed by another mine, and more storage will not help if you habitually leave a large, profitable stockpile undefended.

title: Name the next constraint
text:
Name the next constraint

1. Choose one concrete goal: start the next mine, unlock a colony ship, or fund the next research. Write down the required resources and deadline.

2. Subtract resources already available and place safe incoming deliveries at their scheduled arrival times. Compare the first time each required resource is available, rather than counting a future shipment as current stock.

3. Check whether energy, fields, storage or construction time will block the upgrade. Add the necessary supporting work to the plan.

4. Reserve flight fuel and enough cargo capacity to protect the remaining resources. Spend only the balance.

Resource value is contextual
A metal-heavy account saving for crystal-heavy research should not blindly choose the biggest metal production increase. Reducing the actual waiting time can matter more than a tidy mine ratio.

title: Compare the complete investment
text:
Compare the complete investment

For an income upgrade, divide its full cost by the additional daily income it enables. Keep unlike resources separate unless you explicitly choose a conversion ratio for planning. That ratio is an assumption, not a guaranteed trade offer. Include required energy infrastructure and subtract additional operating costs where relevant.

Compare the next level on several planets, not just your largest planet. A small improvement to a developing colony may be easier to fund and leave the account less dependent on one location. Do not call a facility a bad investment simply because it has no direct payback: evaluate the construction delay it removes.

Illustrative payback, not game costs
Upgrade A costs 1,200,000 planning units including its energy support and adds 30,000 units per day: 40 days. Upgrade B costs 800,000 and adds 25,000 per day: 32 days. B has the shorter simple payback. But if B consumes crystal reserved for tomorrow’s colony unlock, delaying it may still be sensible. Neither estimate includes future reinvestment or losses.

title: Make the offline interval affordable
text:
Make the offline interval affordable

Current stock plus hourly production multiplied by hours away is an unconstrained forecast. Compare it with each resource’s storage capacity; once storage fills, that mine stops accumulating more. Include timed deliveries, rewards and queued spending separately. If storage fills too soon, an earlier collection, planned spending or a storage upgrade can prevent the lost production. Storage is a buffer, not a security system.

Solar satellites are ships and can be destroyed. Fusion consumes deuterium. Evaluate energy options with their operational risks and net production rather than only their purchase price. Keep a small written recovery plan for a power loss: which mines can be reduced temporarily and what you would rebuild first.

title: Verify the result
text:
Verify the result

After completion, check actual output, energy balance and the next storage limit. If the gain differs from your estimate, inspect production settings and bonus expiry before making the same purchase elsewhere. End the session with a named next upgrade and a resource target. Avoid filling queues merely because something is affordable; a deliberate empty queue can be better than an irrelevant expense.

title: Compare the change, not the total
text:
Compare the change, not the total

An upgrade earns its return through the difference between the old and new account. For a mine, compare the next level's production with the current level under the same settings. For Plasma or a global Lifeform effect, add the changes across every affected planet. Exclude resource deliveries that would have arrived anyway.

A practical comparison has three lines: the up-front cost; the added daily production; and the new daily operating cost. Include the next required power project, extra fusion fuel and any storage or cargo that is genuinely necessary to use the increase. If the upgrade fits existing spare capacity, do not charge it for infrastructure you already own.

With planning values M = 1, C = 1.5 and D = 3, metal-equivalent value is M + 1.5C + 3D. These weights correspond to a 3:2:1 exchange assumption, not a promised trade. Use the same weights for spending and income. If Deuterium is your operational constraint, test a higher value as well.

Simple payback in days = full incremental cost / additional net daily income. If additional net income is zero or negative, there is no positive simple payback. For a real recovery date, include funding time, construction/research delay and any lost production before completion. Simple payback does not model reinvestment, attacks, bonus expiry or future account growth.

title: A real baseline mine comparison
text:
A real baseline mine comparison

The classic cost of target level L is floor(base cost × growth factor^(L−1)), separately for each resource. Metal Mine costs start at 60 Metal / 15 Crystal and grow ×1.5; Crystal at 48 Metal / 24 Crystal and ×1.6; Deuterium at 225 Metal / 75 Crystal and ×1.5. Metal and Crystal demand 10 × L × 1.1^L energy; Deuterium demands 20 × L × 1.1^L. Economy speed multiplies output, not these power terms. See the formula reference and maintained building reference.

Example assumptions: mines 30/25/25, ×8 economy, slot 8, Tmax +40°C, full production; no class, Plasma, officer, item, Lifeform or crawler effects. Prerequisites are already owned, and at least 781 energy is spare, so each alternative can run without new power. Costs are classic costs before discounts. Income and energy changes are shown before game display rounding.

Metal narrowly wins this deliberately limited comparison. Crystal can still be the sensible next purchase if it is holding up a useful research, and extra power costs could change the order. A colder planet improves the Deuterium candidate; a different position changes the metal/crystal base. Recalculate after every purchase rather than converting this one example into a permanent mine ratio.

Deuterium 25→26 | 5,681,512 / 1,893,837 | 3,994.11 D | 780.10 | 29.63 days

title: Find the actual waiting-time bottleneck
text:
Find the actual waiting-time bottleneck

For a named goal with no future deliveries or spending, subtract resources already available from each required resource and divide each remaining deficit by that resource’s reliable net production. The largest result controls the funding time in that simplified model. A positive deficit with no positive income has no finite waiting time. For an actual schedule, add each delivery only when it arrives, subtract planned spending when it occurs, and find the first time all required balances are available together. Subtracting a future cargo immediately can predict a purchase before its resources arrive.

Suppose the remaining deficits are 200,000 M, 150,000 C and 20,000 D, and net production is 20,000/5,000/2,000 per hour. The waits are 10, 30 and 10 hours. More metal does not shorten the 30-hour crystal wait. Any upgrade bought first also consumes resources and takes time, so compare the whole completion date rather than the new production rate alone.

For example, a 100,000-Crystal goal with no current stock and 5,000 Crystal per hour takes 20 hours without deliveries. If 100,000 Crystal is due after 12 hours, the goal becomes fundable at hour 12, not immediately. A delivery due after 30 hours would not shorten the original 20-hour wait. This example assumes no storage constraint, other spending or delivery loss.

title: Value the storage you will actually use
text:
Value the storage you will actually use

For positive net production, time to full is (capacity − current stock) / hourly production, provided stock is below capacity and no other events intervene. Once a resource reaches its production limit, extending the absence does not keep adding mine income at the old rate. Check each resource separately and include queued costs, incoming cargo and rewards at their actual times. The basic economy reference documents the storage stop.

At 600,000 stock, 1,000,000 capacity and 50,000 per hour, storage fills in eight hours. A twelve-hour absence would lose up to 200,000 production compared with an unconstrained forecast. A larger store is useful if it prevents that recurring loss; an earlier collection can solve the same problem. More storage does not reduce the value an attacker can see sitting on the planet.

title: Plan power around net production.
text: Solar, satellites and fusion at a common demand, with account-wide research, fuel and recovery costs. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.

title: Compare three different power sources
text:
Compare three different power sources

Solar Plants are stable, consume fields and have no deuterium operating bill. Solar Satellites use no building fields but can be destroyed; their output depends on the planet’s maximum temperature. Fusion Reactors use fields and deuterium, but their output scales with both reactor level and Energy Technology. Ordinary attacks do not destroy these buildings.

That is fusion’s late-game advantage: large, durable power output from relatively few fields, especially where cold temperatures make satellites weak. It is not automatically the cheapest starting choice. A small account can reasonably prefer solar while it funds colonies and essential research. A mature mining account should compare fusion seriously before committing to another expensive Solar Plant level or a huge satellite fleet.

title: Baseline power and fuel formulas
text:
Baseline power and fuel formulas

For the standard unmodified formulas, Solar Plant energy = 20 × L × 1.1^L. Fusion energy = 30 × F × (1.05 + 0.01 × E)^F, where L is Solar Plant level, F is Fusion Reactor level and E is Energy Technology level. Full-output fusion fuel use = 10 × F × 1.1^F deuterium per hour at ×1 economy; multiply the fuel use by economy speed. Energy output itself is not multiplied by economy speed.

Energy Technology raises fusion output without raising this baseline reactor fuel bill. It does not improve Solar Plant or satellite output. Because normal research is account-wide, one Energy Technology upgrade benefits reactors on every planet. Evaluate its combined power gain across the whole account, not only the planet paying for the research.
