title: Temperature and satellite scale
text:
Temperature and satellite scale

At Fusion 20, raising Energy Technology from 16 to 20 increases baseline output from 27,155 to 52,041, about 91.6%, with unchanged baseline fuel consumption. At ×8 economy that reactor consumes about 10,764 deuterium per hour, roughly 258,336 per day before modifiers. Compare that expense with the income enabled by the power, not with your total deuterium stock.

For another perspective, at a maximum temperature of +40°C, the baseline satellite formula floor((Tmax + 140) / 6) gives 30 energy per satellite. Matching the 52,041-energy reactor requires 1,735 satellites. At Tmax −90°C, it gives 8 energy and needs 6,506 satellites. Satellites may still be cheaper upfront; the question is whether you want that much power exposed to destruction.

Price the next decision, not the whole past
If you already own Fusion 20 on ten planets, a new Energy Technology level benefits all ten. Compare its cost with ten local reactor upgrades. If you own no reactors, include their construction and the research together. Do not demolish existing solar power simply because a new calculation favors fusion.

title: Price useful power at a common demand
text:
Price useful power at a common demand

Spare energy has no direct sale value. Its benefit is the mine/crawler production it enables, a reactor setting it lets you reduce, a future power purchase it avoids or a reserve against losing temporary supply. Compare alternatives at the same working demand.

For each option, count its additional construction/research cost and its fuel over your planning horizon. Add any replacement allowance and lost production you choose to model, keeping that risk assumption visible. For example, an assumed satellite loss once a year is a scenario, not a measured attack probability. Do not charge existing solar buildings their historical purchase cost again, and do not demolish them merely because new fusion capacity now looks attractive.

At low demand, an affordable Solar Plant level or a manageable satellite batch may preserve resources for colonies and mines. At large demand, field pressure, cold satellites and recurring crawler power make fusion worth comparing. There is no universal mine level at which every account should switch.

title: Research versus one more reactor level
text:
Research versus one more reactor level

For reactor level F and Energy Technology E, baseline power is 30F(1.05 + 0.01E)^F. Raising E by one changes power by the ratio ((1.06 + 0.01E)/(1.05 + 0.01E))^F. The baseline full-load fuel bill stays unchanged. This explains why the same research becomes more valuable across a large reactor network.

At Fusion 20 / Energy 20, baseline output is 52,041.70 energy. Energy 21 raises it to 61,032.64, a 17.28% increase. By comparison, Fusion 21 / Energy 20 gives 68,304.74, but full-load fuel at ×8 rises from about 10,764.00 to 12,432.42 Deuterium per hour. The local building gives a larger local power gain; research benefits every reactor. Their prices and construction/research times are different, so output alone does not choose the winner.

If ten identical reactors are present, the Energy 20→21 gain is about 89,909 energy across the account, distributed across those ten planets. It cannot be transferred between planets. A planet without a reactor gains no fusion power. Use each local demand to decide how much of the gain is useful.

title: Turn power into a net-resource comparison
text:
Turn power into a net-resource comparison

Record total energy balance and final net Deuterium under the old settings. Then compare the proposed workload with the same mine levels and active bonuses. Fusion fuel scales with economy speed; a universe's ship-fuel reduction must not be borrowed as a reactor discount. Apply only bonuses that actually affect the power or fuel line concerned.

An illustrative crawler change adds 9,600 M, 5,760 C and 2,880 D per hour, but needs another 4,000 D per hour of fusion fuel. The retained change is +9,600 M, +5,760 C and −1,120 D. At M1/C1.5/D3 that is +14,880 metal-equivalent per hour, or 357,120 per day. If the incremental power investment costs 10,000,000 in those same units, its simple payback is about 28.00 days. A positive total value can coexist with a worsening fuel shortage; check both the valuation and the actual Deuterium reserve.

title: Switch in a controlled sequence
text:
Switch in a controlled sequence

1. Record current energy demand, normal net deuterium income and the next mine/crawler demand. Set a fuel reserve you will not consume.

2. Check the live prerequisites: Fusion requires Deuterium Synthesizer 5 and Energy Technology 3. Price the intended reactor and research levels.

3. Build enough new capacity before reducing existing supply. Keep mines powered during the transition.

4. Adjust fusion operation only as needed and verify the resource screen. The table models full output, not every partial-output setting.

5. Check net production after bonus expiries and after a satellite loss. Revisit the next Energy Technology level across all reactors.

6. For an established reactor network, test whether the new Energy Technology level lets you lower reactor operation while meeting the same demand. Compare the resulting net deuterium on every planet; spare energy is not the only benefit.

Read total energy, not just the satellite row
Bonuses can appear separately from base satellite output. When checking a safe proposed change, compare the total energy balance and all affected bonus rows. Do not invent an extra slot-15 penalty or assume the satellite base row already includes every bonus.

title: Leave a workable recovery setting
text:
Leave a workable recovery setting

Check the account after an energy item expires, a relevant officer expires, class changes, or satellites are lost. A small positive surplus supported by a temporary bonus is not durable capacity. If power becomes short, compare reducing crawler overload or a noncritical mine while restoring supply; do not assume buying more mine levels solves the deficit. Keep a reserve for flight fuel and the resources needed to rebuild the chosen power source.

A higher Energy Technology level may permit a lower reactor setting while preserving full production. Verify the actual available settings and net fuel change in Resources. This guide does not assume that a continuous optimization formula exactly reproduces current slider and rounding behavior.

title: The decision rule
text:
The decision rule

Prefer fusion when durable power and field efficiency solve a real constraint, the shared research investment is affordable, and net income remains attractive after fuel. Prefer or retain solar when it meets your present demand cheaply, or when the fusion investment would delay more valuable growth. A mixed supply is valid: existing solar can reduce reactor workload while fusion provides the scalable backbone.

title: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text: All fifteen slots, field and temperature trade-offs, and the full investment behind another colony. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.

title: Decide what the colony is for
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Decide what the colony is for

A new planet is an investment with several costs: the research that opens capacity, the colony ship, the flight, startup resources and the time spent developing it. Name the purpose first. It could be additional production, a shorter supply route, a deployment partner or access to another area. A good location for one purpose can be poor for another.

Do not copy a coordinate pattern without considering your fleet speed and login schedule. A distant colony can make deliveries inconvenient; a tightly clustered account may be convenient but offer fewer operating areas. Neither layout is universally correct.

title: Check capacity and prerequisites
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Check capacity and prerequisites

Use the current Astrophysics panel and technology tree to confirm that another planet is allowed and that the intended position can be colonized. The colony ship requires Shipyard 4 and Impulse Drive 3. The October 2026 administrator guide lists its cost as 10,000 metal, 20,000 crystal and 10,000 deuterium. Include the missing prerequisites and flight fuel in your own budget.

Do not interpret an empty slot as proof that your account can settle it. Check capacity again after any other colonization mission resolves. This guide deliberately does not prescribe a maximum planet count or a universal class bonus: the live interface is the final check.

title: Compare candidate locations
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Compare candidate locations

The October 2026 colonisation guide identifies these broad position differences. Planet temperature affects solar satellites and deuterium production, not Solar Plant output. Check the generated planet and your universe field bonus rather than assuming the best possible roll.

1. Make a shortlist of empty positions in areas that fit the colony’s role. Note supply distance and useful nearby planets or moons.

2. Check the surrounding activity. Look for active neighbors and whether your proposed logistics would be comfortable to operate, not merely possible.

3. Compare the position’s production and temperature implications using current game information. Do not assume proximity to the sun improves every energy source.

4. Estimate the first supply shipment and its timing. Keep your main account’s next essential upgrade and fleetsave fuel funded.

5. Recheck the destination immediately before launching the colonization mission. Record when you will be available to inspect the result.

Position tendency | What it helps | Tradeoff to investigate
Slots 1–3 | Crystal production bonuses | Small planets and extra Astrophysics requirements
Slots 6–10 | Metal bonuses and generally larger planets | Compare supply routes; slot 8 has the largest metal bonus
Slot 15 | Cold temperatures favor deuterium | Small planets, weak satellite output and extra Astrophysics requirements

title: Apply field bonuses in the right place
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Apply field bonuses in the right place

Base fields derive from planet diameter squared: (diameter / 1,000)^2. Discoverer’s 10% and the Researchers alliance class’s 5% colonization bonuses affect diameter, not fields directly. The 2026 official example turns a 15,000-km, 225-field base planet into 297 fields with both bonuses. Universe extra fields are then added separately. Do not apply a 15% field increase instead.

Lifeform buildings and field items can alter the usable result after settlement; do not treat them as guaranteed base colonization size. The Lifeforms FAQ specifically warns that leaving Kaelesh removes Bio Modifier bonus fields. Reserve room for the infrastructure your plan needs rather than accepting a tight colony only because a temporary setup makes it appear roomy.

Position bonuses increase the mine-production base used by subsequent production bonuses. Do not simply add the position percentage to all other percentage bonuses. For example, unmodified Metal production of 1,000 becomes a slot-8 base of 1,350. A separate 10% mine-production bonus then contributes 135 rather than 100. This isolates the position interaction; a full account calculation must still apply the other bonuses correctly.

A practical slot choice
For a metal-focused general mining planet, slot 8 offers +35% base metal and a 156–252 base-field range. Slot 1 offers +40% crystal but only 96–172 base fields and much warmer temperatures. Neither bonus describes total account income. Choose according to the resource you need, your field plan, and the energy system you can support.

title: Inspect before heavily investing
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Inspect before heavily investing

The generated planet must be evaluated after arrival. Review its fields, temperature and how it serves the intended role. Set a reasonable acceptance criterion before launching, so you do not endlessly reroll looking for a mythical perfect planet. If it does not meet your needs, pause major spending and compare alternatives. Abandonment is a separate, consequential decision; check its warnings and all assets first.

Ships accompanying colonization are not automatically a permanent local fleet. The administrator guide notes that accompanying ships return after delivering resources. If you need cargo ships stationed there, arrange a separate deployment and verify the mission type.

Illustrative expansion budget
Suppose research and prerequisites need 700,000 resource units, the ship and travel budget need 50,000, and initial development needs 250,000. Your expansion costs 1,000,000 in this planning example, not merely 50,000. If you have only 800,000 available after fuel reserves, postpone optional development or save more before committing.

title: Develop in stages and connect the route
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Develop in stages and connect the route

First establish usable production and the energy to support it. Then add only the facilities required by the colony’s next job. Send startup resources in manageable waves rather than leaving the entire future build budget on an undeveloped planet. Do not neglect the supplier while funding the new world.

Treat the colony as operational when it can contribute resources, receive supplies and participate in your safety plan without constant emergency fixes. Test a small transfer, check available cargo and note its next storage deadline. Review the colony after a few sessions: is it reducing a bottleneck, or have you created a location that continually consumes attention without meeting its intended purpose?

title: Capacity and location are separate gates
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Capacity and location are separate gates

The research-only baseline is one homeworld plus floor((Astrophysics + 1)/2) colonies. Astrophysics 1 opens the first colony, then each odd level opens another. Positions 4–12 are available at level 1; 3 and 13 at level 4; 2 and 14 at level 6; 1 and 15 at level 8. An empty position still requires both an available colony slot and sufficient Astrophysics. Additional account entitlements, if present, are outside this baseline; use the actual capacity shown before launch. See Colonization.

A Colony Ship requires Shipyard 4 and Impulse Drive 3 and costs 10,000 Metal, 20,000 Crystal and 10,000 Deuterium before any applicable changes. Accompanying ships can deliver resources but return rather than becoming a stationed local fleet. Include flight fuel and a separate deployment when establishing local cargo capacity. See the October 2026 administrator guide.

A range is not a guaranteed roll.

At equal mine levels and other relevant bonuses, the colder example produces about 51.61% more gross Deuterium. Within slot 15, −130°C versus −90°C changes the term from 1.80 to 1.96, about 8.89% more. Colder does not make Solar Plants or Fusion Reactors less productive.

title: Slot 8 versus slot 15: a useful comparison
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Slot 8 versus slot 15: a useful comparison

Consider only mine-derived output from equal Metal 30 and Deuterium 25 mines at ×8 economy, with no bonuses except position, and compare slot 8 at Tmax +50°C with slot 15 at −110°C. This comparison excludes natural base income. The slot-8 metal bonus is worth about 43,972.49 M/hour. The colder slot-15 synthesizer gains about 13,868.42 D/hour. In this stripped-down comparison, the mine-income break-even value is about 3.17 Metal per Deuterium.

This is not a universal ranking. Different metal/deuterium levels, Plasma and Lifeform bonuses, actual temperatures and resource values change it. At 3M per D, the slot-8 metal gain is slightly more valuable in this example; at 3.5M per D, the slot-15 Deuterium gain is more valuable before power and field costs. If both planets use the same fusion setup at the same workload, their baseline reactor burn is the same. If one needs additional fuel or replacement satellites, compare the resulting net output instead.

The best slot can still be a poor operational location. Include collection distance, deployment partners, available time and the surroundings. An ideal paper return that requires a supply schedule you cannot maintain is not a reliable return.

title: Fields are a long-term budget
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Fields are a long-term budget

Base fields are derived from diameter, then integer rounding applies. In the official unenhanced example, a 15,000-km planet has 225 base fields. Discoverer's 10% and Researchers' 5% colonization diameter bonuses combine to 17,250 km; floor(17.25²) gives 297 fields. This is not merely 15% more fields. Universe extra fields are added separately. Do not recover an exact original diameter by taking the square root of a rounded field count.

Budget ordinary building levels, not just mines. Mines 40/35/37 use 112 levels of space; Fusion 22 and retained Solar Plant 20 bring that to 154 before robotics, shipyard, laboratories, storage and other facilities. Reserve practical headroom for the next development stage and use the current field display for the final result. Temporary field effects should not be the only reason a permanently cramped colony looks adequate. The Lifeform reference covers species changes and loss of bonus fields.

title: Price expansion as a project
page: Compare planet positions and expansion costs.
text:
Price expansion as a project

Count the remaining Astrophysics levels, missing prerequisites, colony ship, travel, startup mines, power, logistics and any intended Lifeform unlocks. Compare that marginal project with improving an existing planet. Do not charge the whole historical account's research to the new colony, but do include both levels when the next planet requires an even-plus-odd pair.

A new planet can benefit from existing global Lifeform technologies and may later add global bonuses of its own. That can improve expansion economics, but only after the necessary local setup and selected technologies are funded. Use a development schedule rather than crediting a mature colony's full income on its first day. Decide a reasonable field/temperature acceptance range before sending repeated colony ships; perfect-roll hunting has ship, time and opportunity costs too.

title: Choose research by its actual benefit.
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text: Astrophysics thresholds and prices, Plasma returns, and eligible laboratory networks. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.

title: Start with a capability
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Start with a capability

Pick one result you will actually use: a colony ship, additional fleet capacity, a particular ship, or a production improvement. Research levels are means to those results. A long technology list can tempt you to buy one of everything without ever completing a useful chain.

Open the target’s technology tree and write down every unmet prerequisite. Include building levels as well as research levels. Then order them so each requirement becomes available before you need it. Keep this plan short enough to finish; a list of every late-game technology is not a near-term plan.

title: Classify the benefit
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Classify the benefit

Classic research applies across the account. Lifeform technology levels are developed separately on planets, but their applicable active bonuses can contribute across the account. A Research Lab enables technologies and influences research duration. The classic system runs one normal research at a time; a queue schedules work rather than creating parallel classic research. Check current restrictions around laboratory upgrades before starting a long technology.

Unused capacity earns nothing
An extra slot helps only if you can fund and manage the additional mission. Research should match your real activity rather than an idealized day with unlimited time.

Benefit | Question to ask | Evidence of success
Unlock | What action becomes possible? | The ship, mission or building is available
Capacity | Am I consistently reaching this limit? | The extra capacity is used
Efficiency | What recurring cost or delay improves? | A measurable change in a normal session
Prerequisite | What is the next step in the chain? | The intended follow-on research is ready

title: Research costs and prerequisites
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Research costs and prerequisites

1. Write the target, its prerequisites and the resources needed for each missing step. Use current costs from your account.

2. Estimate when the slowest resource will be ready. Account for planned spending elsewhere before promising a start time.

3. Check the lab requirement and displayed duration on the planet where you will start. Compare a lab upgrade only if its total delay and cost are justified.

4. Schedule any lab work before the long research begins, after checking the current queue restrictions.

5. Reserve resources for using the unlock. A newly available ship is not helpful if no budget remains to build it or fuel it.

title: Buy time deliberately
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Buy time deliberately

An expensive lab investment may make sense when you have a sustained research program. It may be wasteful when one affordable unlock is the only immediate objective. Compare the completion date of the entire plan, including the time to fund and construct the lab, rather than only the shorter research timer.

Later, Intergalactic Research Network can combine eligible laboratories; do not assume every lab you own contributes automatically. Read its current description and the technology’s lab requirement before distributing upgrades. The right question is which additional lab actually shortens the research you intend to run.

Illustrative schedule comparison
A technology takes 20 hours now. Preparing a better lab takes 8 hours and reduces that research to 14 hours. For this single goal, 8 + 14 = 22 hours is slower than starting now. If several future researches benefit, the lab may still be worthwhile. Include resource waiting time before deciding.

title: Test the unlocked capability
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Test the unlocked capability

When research finishes, confirm that the intended action is now available. Recalculate relevant fleet times after drive research; an old fleetsave timetable may no longer fit. If you bought mission capacity, try the additional mission during a session you can supervise. If you expected a production gain, compare the resource screen before and after under the same settings.

Record what the upgrade changed and choose the next bottleneck. Do not immediately buy another level by habit. A useful research plan is revised as the account gains colonies, changes play style or loses the time needed to use an active fleet.

title: The recurring benefits worth comparing
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
The recurring benefits worth comparing

These are the classic baseline effects, before applicable class, officer, item and Lifeform changes. Source: staff research reference and maintained research reference. Fleet-specific drive thresholds and combat research belong with the fleet reference.

title: Plasma: the percentage is of the base
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Plasma: the percentage is of the base

Use the applicable mine base, including the appropriate position/economy treatment, rather than multiplying the final total income by the advertised percentage. Additional modifier interactions need their own model; the resource screen is the check for a real account.

Suppose the relevant aggregate hourly bases are 1,000,000 M, 500,000 C and 300,000 D. One Plasma level adds 10,000 M, 3,300 C and 990 D per hour in this unmodified example. At M1/C1.5/D3, the gain is 430,080 metal-equivalent per day.

Classic Plasma level 15 costs 32,768,000 M, 65,536,000 C and 16,384,000 D before reductions. At those weights its cost is 180,224,000 and simple payback about 419.05 days. This is deliberately an illustration of the calculation, not a recommendation for level 15. More planets or higher mines improve the return; a cheaper local upgrade can still win now. If Plasma is not yet unlocked, include the missing prerequisites. The classic prerequisites are Research Lab 4, Energy 8, Laser 10 and Ion 5.

title: Laboratories and IRN: eligibility matters
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Laboratories and IRN: eligibility matters

IRN level N can combine the starting laboratory with up to N additional eligible laboratories. Each contributing lab must meet the minimum lab requirement for the technology being researched. It does not divide one research into parallel independent completions, and it does not let an insufficient starting lab ignore the technology tree.

With laboratories 12, 10 and 8 and IRN 2, a technology requiring Lab 8 can use an effective level of 30. A technology requiring Lab 10 can use only 22. Raising IRN again does not help either example if there is no further eligible lab. Conversely, bringing a nearby lab across an eligibility threshold may contribute its whole level to the network, not just the one new level.

Before modifiers, research time in hours is (Metal cost + Crystal cost) / [1,000 × (1 + effective lab level) × total research speed]. Deuterium is part of the resource price but not this baseline time numerator. For an unchanged research and other factors, increasing effective lab 22→30 changes the timer by 23/31, about 25.81% shorter.

Use the universe's total advertised research multiplier. A server listed as ×10 economy and ×20 research means ×20 in this equation, not ×200. Class, officer, Lifeform and other time modifiers require the actual applicable calculation; compare the final displayed duration before starting. See the October 2026 settings explanation.

title: Time saved is valuable only when the program uses it
page: Choose research by its actual benefit.
text:
Time saved is valuable only when the program uses it

Compare completion dates including funding, laboratory construction and any queue restrictions. Eight hours of lab preparation followed by a fourteen-hour technology completes in twenty-two hours, later than starting its present twenty-hour timer immediately. The lab may still pay off over a longer research program.

For expansion, count the even level that lies between today's odd Astrophysics level and the next colony. For an extra expedition slot, check the square-number threshold and whether normal fleet slots, ships and your schedule can use it. For drive upgrades, recheck future launch timings and fuel rather than assuming your old fleetsave settings still fit.

title: Compare crawler capacity and overload.
text: Working limits, overload energy, production ceilings and net-resource comparisons. Reviewed 9 November 2026. Published baseline mechanics and calculated scenarios; actual modifiers and game rounding must be checked. PTS evidence is identified separately.

title: Understand what you are buying
text:
Understand what you are buying

Crawlers are stationary production support. They cannot accompany a fleetsave, so budget them as vulnerable local infrastructure rather than mobile fleet. The official class FAQ lists Collector as required for construction, with Shipyard 5, Combustion Drive 4, Armour Technology 4 and Laser Technology 4. The base unit cost is 2,000 metal, 2,000 crystal and 1,000 deuterium. Confirm the current technology tree before starting a large queue.

Start with a planet that already has meaningful mine output and reliable power. A crawler bonus on weak mines is small, while its energy requirement still needs funding. Build in batches so you can verify the displayed gain before repeating the purchase across the account.

title: Calculate the working limit
text:
Calculate the working limit

The standard active-count limit is 8 × (Metal Mine level + Crystal Mine level + Deuterium Synthesizer level). Before Lifeform class enhancement, a Collector with an active Geologist has 10% more working capacity. Rock’tal Collector Enhancement can increase that capacity bonus; read the allowed working count in your account. This is not a multiplier from economy speed. Collector’s 50% crawler-output improvement is also not a 50% increase in the number that can work.

Keep three quantities distinct: crawlers owned, crawlers allowed to work, and the production bonus actually realized. A separate 50% crawler-production cap is documented in the official 22 July 2026 PTS 13.0.0-r5 changelog. That is test-server patch evidence, not a fresh measurement of every live universe; confirm the current bonus row in your account. More working capacity does not guarantee more income once that bonus ceiling is reached. Lifeform changes can make the ceiling relevant earlier; inspect the current bonus row rather than blindly filling the count limit.

title: Stop before extra spending stops helping
text:
Stop before extra spending stops helping

Without lifeform modifiers, a Collector at 150% workload gains 0.045% per active crawler before the cap. Thus 1,111 yields 49.995%; 1,112 reaches the 50% ceiling if the mine-based limit permits it. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a universal recommended fleet size. Enhanced efficiency, operating settings and your working limit change the useful number.

If raising the workload or building another batch does not raise the crawler production row, stop and check the cap. Do not assume a production enhancement is broken merely because a capped output remains unchanged. If the higher workload only draws more power, reduce it to the lowest setting that preserves the desired output.

title: Measure the marginal return
text:
Measure the marginal return

In the worked 640-crawler example, moving a Collector from 100% to 150% workload adds 9.6 percentage points of baseline crawler production and 32,000 energy demand. It does not add 50% to the entire planet’s total income. If your relevant mine base were 100,000 metal/hour, the uncapped extra crawler metal would be 9,600/hour before other applicable effects. Repeat for crystal and deuterium, then subtract any extra fusion fuel.

Price the extra energy infrastructure as part of the crawler investment. If you use satellites, include replacement exposure in the decision. If you use fusion, compare a shared Energy Technology upgrade with local reactor levels. There is no reason to overcharge simply because the slider allows it.

title: Add crawlers in verified batches
text:
Add crawlers in verified batches

1. Read mine levels, working limit, current crawler count, energy balance and production bonus on one planet.

2. Check that the next batch fits the active limit and still produces a useful gain below the bonus cap.

3. Fund the energy supply and reserve replacement resources before starting the batch.

4. Compare the resource screen at 100% and at the intended Collector workload. Record net deuterium, not just gross mine output.

5. Recheck after mine upgrades, class changes, Geologist expiry and lifeform changes. Then repeat only where the result is worthwhile.

title: Three limits, three separate questions
text:
Three limits, three separate questions

Crawlers are stationary ships that support local mining. Collector is required to build them under the standard class rules; another class can operate crawlers already owned, with its applicable non-Collector effects. The classic unit costs 2,000 M, 2,000 C and 1,000 D and requires Shipyard 5, Combustion Drive 4, Armour 4 and Laser 4.

Baseline working capacity is 8 × (Metal Mine + Crystal Mine + Deuterium Synthesizer levels). Collector with an active Geologist has 10% more before Lifeform class enhancement. The class's 50% output improvement is a different effect; it does not mean 50% more units may work. See the class FAQ.

- How many are owned?

- How many are allowed to contribute under the mine-based working limit?

- How much of their potential production survives the production ceiling and power constraints?

title: Work through one planet
text:
Work through one planet

Example: mines 30/25/25 total 80 levels. The base active limit is 640; with Collector and Geologist it is 704. The table uses the baseline bonus of 0.02% per crawler, Collector’s ×1.5 output, and no lifeform effects. All rows assume sufficient energy and stay below the 50% bonus ceiling.

150% workload is not 150% energy
The class FAQ states that each 10-point workload increase above 100% costs 20% more energy. At 150% workload, a baseline 50-energy crawler needs 100 energy. Lifeform reductions must be applied separately.

Setup | Working crawlers | Crawler bonus | Energy draw
Non-Collector operating owned crawlers, 100% workload | 640 | 12.80% | 32,000
Collector, 100% workload | 640 | 19.20% | 32,000
Collector, 150% workload | 640 | 28.80% | 64,000
Collector + Geologist, 150% workload | 704 | 31.68% | 70,400

title: Overload buys output at a worse marginal power rate
text:
Overload buys output at a worse marginal power rate

The no-Lifeform baseline is 0.02% of the relevant mine base per working crawler at 100%, multiplied by 1.5 for Collector. At Collector 150%, one crawler contributes 0.045% before the production ceiling. It does not add 0.045% to the final already-boosted planet total.

The overload increments add 10% of the 100%-setting output for another 20% of its baseline energy. At 150%, output is 1.5 times the 100% result while power is twice as high. That does not make overload automatically bad: spare or efficient power can justify it. It does mean a power-constrained planet should compare its net return, not simply select the largest number.

Collector workload | Bonus per active crawler before cap | Baseline energy per crawler
100% | 0.030% | 50
110% | 0.033% | 60
120% | 0.036% | 70
130% | 0.039% | 80
140% | 0.042% | 90
150% | 0.045% | 100

title: The production ceiling can arrive before the count limit
text:
The production ceiling can arrive before the count limit

The official July 22, 2026 PTS r5 changelog explicitly records restoring a 50% mine-production cap. That source is PTS evidence, not a new measurement on every live universe. Use the current Resources bonus and energy rows when deciding how many units or what workload is useful.

With no Lifeform effects, Collector at 150% gives 1,111 × 0.045% = 49.995%; the 1,112th crawler would cross a 50% ceiling if the count limit permits it. A UI rounded to 50.00% can conceal that small difference, so use actual output as well as the printed percentage. Class enhancement, Ion Crystal Modules and other relevant effects change the useful count; do not apply this number as a universal target.

If the production row stops increasing while energy demand rises, a higher workload is buying no additional mine income. Use the lowest available setting that retains the desired output. Do not assume an efficiency technology is useless merely because production is capped: an independent energy reduction can still matter. Exact Lifeform stacking is covered separately; the baseline table here deliberately excludes it.

title: Count the retained resources
text:
Count the retained resources

For 640 Collector crawlers, 100→150% adds 9.6 percentage points of the relevant mine base and 32,000 energy demand. With bases of 100,000 M, 60,000 C and 30,000 D per hour, the uncapped extra gross production is 9,600 M, 5,760 C and 2,880 D per hour.

Now price the power that actually supplies those 32,000 units. Additional fusion fuel reduces net Deuterium; satellite supply adds destruction and replacement exposure; a shared Energy Technology upgrade may help several planets. The linked power example shows how positive metal-equivalent income can still worsen the Deuterium fuel balance. If power is short, compare the whole planet before and after, because reduced mine production can outweigh the crawler gain.

Recheck after a mine upgrade, class change, Geologist expiry, energy bonus expiry or a Lifeform change. Do not copy one planet's working count and workload to every colony without comparing its mines, power and actual return.

title: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text: A practical reference for choosing a route and handling its return. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: Protect the return, not only the departure
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Protect the return, not only the departure

Fleetsaving means moving ships and movable resources off a location during your absence. The dangerous moment is often the landing: another player may arrange an attack to arrive immediately afterward. Defenses can discourage a casual raid but do not make a valuable fleet safe.

Decide when you can genuinely be online before choosing a route. Use the game’s arrival display and server clock, not an estimate from yesterday. Research, ship composition and speed settings can change the duration. Leave time to reconnect, inspect events and act; an alarm at the landing second is too late.

title: Choose a method you understand
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Choose a method you understand

Without a moon, deployment between your own planets is a useful route to understand. Its outbound movement appears on a phalanx scan of the destination planet, not the origin. A recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx, although observations made before recall can help an opponent estimate its return. Deployment to an owned moon has no directly scannable destination. With two suitable moons, moon-to-moon Deployment avoids direct phalanx scans at both endpoints, but moon destruction, predictable habits and an unattended arrival remain risks.

Transport is not deployment
Transport unloads and returns. Deployment stations the ships at the destination unless recalled. Verify the mission name and both location types, not just the coordinates.

Situation | Practical approach | What still needs attention
Two planets, no moon | Practice deployment and recall with a small fleet | Outbound visible at destination; recall timing may be inferred
Suitable pair of moons | Plan a moon-to-moon deployment | Moon destruction; arrival security
Only one useful departure point | Get an alliance review of available routes | Do not assume any long mission is safe

title: Run the departure checklist
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Run the departure checklist

1. Gather the ships you intend to protect. Check outstanding returns and shipyard completions that could leave ships behind after departure.

2. Select the destination and confirm whether each end is a planet or moon. Pick deployment only when that is your intended method.

3. Set speed and read the resulting arrival time. For a recalled save, first practice and inspect the return timer with a small, expendable fleet.

4. Load resources within capacity, accounting for flight fuel. Make sure the destination or return location will have what you need for the next launch.

5. Send, then reopen the event list. Confirm the mission exists with the expected ships, cargo and time. A clicked button is not proof of launch.

title: Plan around real life
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Plan around real life

Use two reminders if helpful: one before you need to log in and one before the critical event. An unreliable connection is a reason for more margin, not tighter timing. If you cannot reliably cover any return window, investigate vacation mode and its current conditions before the absence. It is not an emergency button to assume will fix an already developing attack.

Illustrative schedule
You expect to be home at 18:00 but might be delayed 30 minutes. A landing at 18:05 is a poor plan. Select a route that gives you a comfortable margin after the latest realistic return, then confirm its exact timing in game. If your schedule changes, reassess before leaving rather than hoping the old plan still fits.

title: Recall timing and threat response
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Recall timing and threat response

Do one small deployment while you stay online. Inspect its outbound event, recall it, and observe the displayed return. Repeat with the ship mix you normally use, because the slowest ship affects travel. This is a route check, not a promise of invulnerability.

When threatened, first read the incoming mission and time. Do not recall in panic without checking whether you can cover the resulting return. Ask an experienced ally to review the precise situation privately. Do not publish live fleet coordinates or return times in a public alliance guide. After every save, inspect the original location for leftovers and new production.

title: Match the mission to the exposure
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Match the mission to the exposure

Deployment remains the useful starting point because its outbound movement and recall have different visibility rules. With two suitable moons, a deployment avoids direct phalanx scans at both endpoints. Without moons, a deployment to another owned planet can be inspected at the receiving planet. Recalling removes that deployment from phalanx, but earlier scans may still help an observer estimate its return.

The important comparison is not simply moon versus planet. Check the mission, both endpoint types, which part of the flight is underway, and what happens if a moon disappears. The matrix below describes ordinary visibility before such changes.

Route or phase | Ordinary phalanx exposure | Practical consequence
Planet → planet Deployment | Destination planet, not departure planet | Be present before arrival; understand recall timing.
Planet → moon Deployment | Neither the departure planet nor target moon reveals that Deployment directly | A planet origin does not make every mission visible; moon loss still changes the route.
Moon → planet Deployment | Destination planet | The moon origin does not hide arrival at a planet.
Moon → moon Deployment | Neither moon is a scannable target | Watch the moons and the landing window.
Recalled Deployment | Absent from phalanx at both ends | Hidden on scans does not erase previously observed timing.
Transport or attack involving a planet | Eligible planet endpoint can reveal movement | A recall is not the Deployment-recall exception.
Moon → debris-field harvest | No directly scannable endpoint | Debris disappearance and predictable routines can still expose timing.

title: Two deployment routines, two commitments
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Two deployment routines, two commitments

An arrival save ends with ships stationed at the destination. Plan to be present before they land, with the destination inspected and the next move already affordable. This is the simpler routine to understand, but a visible destination arrival can become a target.

A planned recall save adds a second commitment: you must recall before the original arrival and then cover the newly displayed return. Decide on that window before departure. The best route is not the one that produces the longest flight; it is the one whose required actions you can reliably perform.

Practise with a small fleet while online. Record the displayed outbound arrival, recall it at a known time, and check the actual return. Do not use a generic stopwatch rule for a valuable fleet when the live event list can tell you the result. Changing research, bonuses, composition or speed can invalidate an old preset.

After recall, the return is the commitment
Do not assume you can recall a recalled fleet again. Confirm the new landing window immediately. Recalling simply because an attack looks frightening can exchange a manageable situation for a return you cannot supervise.

title: When a moon disappears
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
When a moon disappears

Moon destruction can redirect a moon-related flight to the associated planet. That can create a scannable endpoint where none existed before. Re-read the event list after the loss instead of relying on the route you originally launched.

A player-recalled Deployment keeps its special phalanx treatment; do not apply that exception to every returning Transport, harvest or attack. Conversely, absence from a scan does not prove that an opponent lacks a return estimate. If someone observed the outbound Deployment and the moment it disappeared, they may have enough information to attempt a timed return hit.

Version caveat: a 22 September 2021 staff reply described a Deployment already en route from a planet to its own moon when the moon was destroyed: on reaching the missing destination, it automatically returned to the planet and became phalanx-visible. Live version 12.0.36, released on 27 March 2025, later included moon-loss Deployment visibility fixes, but its notes do not identify this exact same-coordinate case. The current-version behavior of that automatic return has not been verified. Do not assume an automatic return behaves like a player-initiated recall; recheck the actual route and landing.

The live March 2026 change slows Moon Destruction through a fixed Deathstar speed of 310, independent of normal server fleet speed and higher Hyperspace Drive. It buys time in some situations, not immunity. Other Deathstar missions use their normal speed rules. Check the incoming mission itself before estimating your response window.

title: Prepare the landing, including everything left behind
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Prepare the landing, including everything left behind

1. List the protected fleet, resources, outstanding returns and unfinished shipyard batches. Satellites, crawlers and defense are stationary assets and need their own protection and replacement plan.

2. Reserve enough fleet slots, local fuel and transport capacity for the next move. A fleet that has landed safely but cannot leave is still exposed.

3. Before logging off, reopen the event list and check the actual mission, planet/moon types, fleet composition and time. Inspect the launch location for ships or resources you missed.

4. Log in with a margin before the earliest relevant landing. Review all arrivals, not just the main fleet. Delayed expeditions and returning supply cargo may need separate handling.

5. If the schedule changes, reassess while there is still a choice. Plan longer absences ahead using the current vacation-mode conditions. Do not depend on an emergency setting to undo an attack already being resolved.

title: Common shortcuts that fail
page: Fleetsaving: route visibility and failure modes
text:
Common shortcuts that fail

These are risk checks, not guarantees. Keep operational coordinates, fleet sizes, recall times and screenshots in private alliance channels rather than in the public guide.

Shortcut | Why it fails | Better question
Park behind a very large defense | The stationary fleet can make a larger attack worthwhile. | What value will be stationary during my absence?
Launch any long mission | Attacks face combat; expeditions can lose ships or change timing; transport returns automatically. | What can happen before the fleet comes back?
Use the same debris field every night | harvest time can become observable. | What evidence reveals my route or schedule?
Jump to a remote moon and log out | The ships remain stationary after the jump. | What protects the next landing and departure?
Trust the timer without checking the mission | A planet and its moon share coordinates but are different destinations. | Which exact location and mission did I send?

title: Expedition fleet sizing and tradeoffs
text: Calculate value, carrying space, slots and replacement exposure separately. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: What an expedition actually does
text:
What an expedition actually does

An expedition sends a fleet to position 16, holds there to explore, resolves an event and returns surviving ships. It is a chance-based income activity, not a raid on another player. Unlock Astrophysics 1 to start. Its baseline simultaneous-expedition allowance is floor(square root of Astrophysics): levels 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25 allow 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 respectively, before extra slots.

You also need an available ordinary fleet slot. Expedition capacity and total mission capacity are separate limits: an unused expedition allowance does not help when all fleet slots are busy. Discoverer, Admiral and slot items can add capacity; inspect the current totals before planning a batch.

Outcome family | What it means for your plan
Resources or ships | Income varies; resources need available cargo capacity
Dark Matter, items or other special finds | Separate reward rules; do not value everything as spendable metal
Nothing useful | A normal possible result, not proof that the fleet is wrong
Pirates or aliens | Combat can damage or destroy ships
Fleet loss / black hole | The working fleet can be lost entirely
Timing event | Arrival can differ from the ordinary schedule

title: Build the slot count correctly
text:
Build the slot count correctly

The October 2026 administrator guide lists these additions to the Astrophysics-based expedition limit. Ordinary fleet slots are a separate constraint: having enough expedition slots does not guarantee enough free fleet slots to launch them. Recheck the displayed limit when bonuses or items expire.

Source | Additional expedition slots | Condition
Discoverer class | +2 | While Discoverer is active
Admiral | +1 | While the officer is active
Bronze / Silver / Gold expedition-slot items | +1 / +2 / +3 | Different tiers can combine for +6 while active
Kaelesh Discoverer Enhancement | +1 per 50% enhancement | For the active Discoverer; verify the current total

title: Record the account you are calculating for
text:
Record the account you are calculating for

Expedition fleet recommendations are conditional. Record your class, economy speed, relevant research and lifeform bonuses, available expedition slots and the current top-player points bracket. These affect the useful fleet size or the number of missions you can run. The October 2026 OGame US administrator guide recommends a calculator instead of a fixed cargo count.

Verify that any calculator supports your current game version and modifiers. A mathematically precise answer based on the wrong class is still wrong. Save the input assumptions next to the result so you know when to recalculate.

Current-version support matters especially for non-Discoverer comparisons. October 2026 Orion test notes extended economy scaling to Collector and General. The November live rollout confirms version 13.1 but does not separately resolve that expedition change for every older universe. Do not present the old non-Discoverer formula as a universal current rule.

title: Separate reward value from cargo capacity
text:
Separate reward value from cargo capacity

Two questions determine a useful fleet: is its expedition value sufficient for the relevant reward bracket, and can it carry the resource find? They are not the same statistic. The classic expedition points use base structural value, equivalent to the fleet’s Metal-plus-Crystal construction cost divided by 200; Armour Technology does not increase this build-value statistic. Above the useful point threshold, extra ships do not indefinitely raise the reward cap. Cargo capacity is a separate ceiling on what the returning ships can hold.

A Pathfinder provides the expedition reward multiplier described in the official guide; adding more Pathfinders does not repeatedly double that multiplier. More cargo can prevent a large find being truncated, but excess ships add fuel and loss exposure. A probe helps you read depletion, not multiply the reward.

Illustrative cargo check
If your current calculation permits a 12-million resource find but the selected fleet has only 8-million available cargo, that fleet cannot bring home all 12 million. Increasing capacity to cover the find solves that bottleneck. Increasing it to 30 million does not make the reward cap 30 million. Recalculate expedition value and cargo separately.

title: Build a replaceable working fleet
text:
Build a replaceable working fleet

A practical starting concept is cargo capacity supported by a Pathfinder when available and an Espionage Probe for depletion information. The official guide also discusses a single strong combat ship for the find pool. Check the recommended composition against your unlocks and risk tolerance before copying it. Sending your entire battle fleet is not a substitute for calculating the expedition requirement.

Treat every expedition fleet as something you may lose. Keep essential transport ships and fleetsave capacity outside the expedition budget. If losing one launch would strand your account’s resources, make the working fleet smaller or build a replacement reserve first.

title: Fleet verification before expansion
text:
Fleet verification before expansion

1. Select an expedition destination at position 16 and confirm that the mission is Expedition. Review the selected ships and cargo capacity.

2. Choose holding time and speed together. Read the complete schedule and ensure you can cover a delayed return rather than only the normal one.

3. Launch a single test mission. Keep enough capacity and fuel at home for ordinary logistics.

4. Read the full report, including depletion information. Check the returning fleet and actual cargo rather than only the headline reward.

5. Only then fill additional expedition slots that fit your available attention and replacement budget.

An expedition is not a guaranteed overnight fleetsave
Events can delay the return or destroy ships. Keep your main fleet safety plan separate from your expedition income plan.

title: Avoid the two common scheduling traps
text:
Avoid the two common scheduling traps

The administrator guide states that longer holding time increases the chance of an event, not the maximum reward, and can increase delays. Do not extend a hold merely because you want a bigger payout. Depletion at a system’s position 16 is shared with other players; use reports to decide when to vary destinations.

The practical goal is a schedule you can repeat. A theoretically high number of launches means little if ships sit unattended after returning or you repeatedly miss your final collection. Plan the last batch backward from the time you want to stop playing, with room for disruption.

title: Keep a simple performance log
text:
Keep a simple performance log

For a batch, record launches, elapsed time, resource finds, useful ship finds, fuel consumed and losses. Count ship value separately from spendable resources unless you have a realistic way to use or convert those ships. A large ship find does not automatically fund tomorrow’s crystal-heavy research.

Illustrative batch accounting
Twenty launches return 12 million resources, use 1 million in fuel and lose ships costing 3 million. The simplified net is 8 million resource units before any conversion assumptions. That is 400,000 per launch, not the 600,000 suggested by gross rewards. This example is bookkeeping, not an expected OGame return.

title: Change one thing at a time
text:
Change one thing at a time

Review a meaningful batch rather than reacting to a single black hole or exceptional reward. Change one input, such as cargo capacity or destination rotation, and note why. Recheck the calculation after class changes, substantial bonuses or a new points bracket. Do not spend your entire reserve chasing the best recent result. Stable logistics and the ability to replace a lost working fleet matter more than a spectacular screenshot.

title: Keep the assumptions with the fleet recipe
text:
Keep the assumptions with the fleet recipe

A copied fleet count is useful only when its assumptions match yours. Record the universe and game version, player class, economy and peaceful-flight speeds, the top player’s points bracket, Hyperspace Technology, applicable Lifeform and class enhancements, actual ship cargo, slot bonuses and active expedition items.

Also record whether the calculator is sizing for the largest resource find, ship finds, or a smaller risk budget. Those are different objectives. Proxyforgame’s current page has separate resource, ship and class bonus inputs and a resource-discovery booster input; treating all of them as a single percentage can give the wrong answer. Its page currently identifies itself as OGame 13.0, so verify support for later changes before relying on a result.

title: Value qualifies the fleet; cargo carries the result
text:
Value qualifies the fleet; cargo carries the result

The classic expedition-point calculation uses base ship structural value: combined Metal and Crystal divided by 200. Small Cargo contributes 20 points and Large Cargo 60. Armour Technology changes combat durability, not the base build value used for this calculation.

For a simple comparison, fifteen Small Cargos and five Large Cargos each cost 30,000 Metal plus 30,000 Crystal and each provide 300 expedition points. Before bonuses, however, their carrying spaces are 75,000 and 125,000. Equal points and equal construction cost therefore do not mean equal cargo. Speed, drive level, fuel and hostile encounters still need their own comparison.

Extra cargo can prevent a large resource find being truncated. Once both the useful expedition-value threshold and available carrying-space requirement are met, adding ships does not keep raising the same capped reward. It does increase the amount exposed to a full-fleet loss.

Translate a capacity target into ships
If a calculation requires 120,000,000 free carrying space and each Large Cargo actually contributes 37,500, the cargo-only quotient is 3,200 ships. That is a capacity calculation, not a complete expedition recipe: include support ships, loaded resources and the actual dispatch screen before treating it as a launch count.

title: A baseline multiplier example, with its limits
text:
A baseline multiplier example, with its limits

The older official class FAQ gives a baseline Discoverer reward multiplier of 1.5 times economy speed, doubled again when at least one Pathfinder is present. Thus an eight-times-economy Discoverer with a Pathfinder has a baseline factor 24 before Lifeform or item modifiers. The Pathfinder factor is present once, rather than doubling again for each Pathfinder.

The archived table assigns a 5,000,000 Metal base maximum to the bracket above 100 million top-player points. In this deliberately unboosted example, 5,000,000 × 24 gives 120,000,000 Metal. This is a possible ceiling under those baseline assumptions, not an average find or a promise for a current account. A fresh universe may be in a much smaller bracket.

Do not reuse the old non-Discoverer multiplier as a universal live rule. October 2026 Orion test notes extended economy scaling to Collector and General. November’s live deployment announcements confirm version 13.1 and limit Orion activation to new universes, but do not separately document whether that expedition change is enabled on every older universe. Check the target universe and a supported calculation before making a class-switch comparison.

title: Choose support ships for a specific benefit
text:
Choose support ships for a specific benefit

The Deathstar option belongs to advanced tradeoff analysis. Avoiding one event family does not turn an expedition into a safe place for irreplaceable ships. Compare extra cycle time and full-loss exposure before considering it; the ordinary cargo-led working fleet remains easier to replace.

Ship finds join the returning fleet; they are not a box of resources that automatically pays for the next upgrade. Keep usable ships, unwanted ships and resource income separate in your records.

Choice | Benefit to evaluate | Cost or limitation
One Pathfinder | Reward multiplier | Additional Pathfinders do not repeat the multiplier.
One Espionage Probe | Depletion information in the report | It does not make the rewards larger.
One suitable combat ship | The ship-finding pool supported by that composition | Do not interpret strongest as a reason to send the battle fleet.
Small versus Large Cargo | Speed, cargo per investment, fuel and losses | The answer depends on drives, bonuses and actual relaunch opportunities.
A Deathstar | Suppresses pirate and alien encounters under the live 8.5 rule | Very slow and expensive; black-hole loss remains possible.

title: Turn slots and speed into actual daily launches
text:
Turn slots and speed into actual daily launches

At Astrophysics 16, the baseline expedition allowance is 4. With Discoverer(+2), Admiral(+1) and an active Silver slot item(+2), the example allowance becomes 9, before other bonuses. Nine expeditions still need nine available ordinary fleet slots. Leave capacity for necessary transport, scouting and safety rather than discovering that the last launch has consumed all flexibility.

Expedition travel uses peaceful flight speed, but ordinary holding time is not divided by that speed. Plan total cycle time as outbound flight + selected hold + return flight, then add operational slack for events and for the time you are not online to relaunch.

For a simplified schedule, 20 minutes outbound + 60 minutes holding +20 minutes home is 100 minutes. Reducing each travel leg to 15 minutes makes 90 minutes, a 10% cycle reduction, not 25%. Over a continuous eight-hour window, the theoretical completed-cycle counts are 4 and 5. In a real workday, both may still yield only three launches if the return times fall between your logins. Buy the improvement your schedule can use.

title: Treat risk, debris and events as separate systems
text:
Treat risk, debris and events as separate systems

Expedition combat enemies scale with the expedition fleet, so adding military value also changes the encounter you may face. The October 2026 administrator guide reports a combat-debris cap of 20 million per resource type. This is not a guaranteed 60-million return, and resource eligibility and collection still matter. Older uncapped pirate-hunting plans should not be copied into a modern income routine.

A black hole can remove an entire working fleet. Keep the resources or ships needed to rebuild at least the amount of expedition capacity your plan depends on. If that reserve is unaffordable, a smaller fleet or fewer simultaneous launches may be a better choice than stretching to every slot.

Resource/ship bonuses, Dark Matter events, item-find limits and slot items are different mechanics. Read the current event announcement and expiry time. A nine-times-Dark-Matter event does not mean nine-times-resource finds, and a temporary extra slot creates a temporary operating opportunity rather than permanent capacity.

title: Measure the operation without disguising its costs
text:
Measure the operation without disguising its costs

Record launch count, resources by type, usable ship value, flight fuel, lost ships, actual cycle times and time left idle after return. Track losses even on days when the headline reward was unusually good. Decide on a consistent resource valuation before combining Metal, Crystal and Deuterium into one figure.

A useful performance record answers a decision: whether capacity is clipping finds, another slot can be used, a speed change creates an extra cycle, or a reward upgrade beats a mine project. It does not need a claim that one week establishes the true probability of a rare event.

A replacement reserve is a separate budget
If a working fleet costs 9 million planning units and you operate six, 54 million is exposed when all six are flying. Keeping 9 million available allows one immediate replacement, not six. That reserve is liquidity, not a deduction from every launch’s profit unless it is actually spent.

title: Moonshot budgeting and special cases
text: Keep debris math, probability, item handling and moon development separate. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: Choose the job before choosing the location
text:
Choose the job before choosing the location

A moon is a separate location attached to a planet, with its own ships, resources and construction. It enables a Sensor Phalanx and, when paired with another owned moon, a Jump Gate. A planet can have one moon. You obtain it through a qualifying battle at that planet rather than by sending a Colony Ship.

Choose a location you will actually use: a collection hub, a route between your own locations, or a system from which phalanx coverage is valuable. Write down the purpose and the budget for developing the moon afterward. A moonshot that consumes all your transport capacity and fuel can leave the new location unusable.

title: Size the battle for the universe you play
text:
Size the battle for the universe you play

The conventional debris-based chance is one percentage point per complete 100,000 units of qualifying battle debris, capped at a 20% base chance. Use the debris produced by that battle, not old debris already at the coordinates. The standard target is therefore 2,000,000 debris. Event and Lifeform modifiers can raise the actual chance; 20% is not an absolute modern ceiling.

For an ordinary all-Light-Fighter shot, each destroyed fighter contributes 4,000 × f debris, where f is the ship-to-debris fraction. Required fighters = round up [2,000,000 ÷ (4,000 × f)]. This assumes all those fighters are destroyed and does not count extra losses on the receiving side. Simulate the exact battle.

A probability is not a promise
At a constant 20% chance, the probability of at least one success in n independent attempts is 1 − 0.8ⁿ. Five attempts give 67.23%; ten give 89.26%. Five failures do not make the next shot more likely. Set a maximum loss budget before trying again.

Ship debris setting | Light Fighters for 20% base | Debris if all are destroyed
30% | 1,667 | 2,000,400
50% | 1,000 | 2,000,000
70% | 715 | 2,002,000
80% | 625 | 2,000,000

title: Prepare a controlled moonshot
text:
Prepare a controlled moonshot

1. Confirm the receiving planet has no moon, the debris setting, the current event window and the participants’ combat technologies. Agree on the exact coordinates, impact time, fleet composition and who will recover the debris.

2. Check the current rules for your community and universe before agreeing compensation. A friendly shot does not exempt transfers from pushing restrictions. If the arrangement is unclear, resolve it with support before the battle rather than relying on a years-old moonshot rule.

3. Simulate enough defending fleet or defense to destroy the intended shot. Include rapid fire, technologies and relevant bonuses. Move unrelated valuable ships and excess resources away from the receiving planet.

4. Arrange recycler capacity and timing, and keep the necessary defenders present until impact. A simulator estimates an outcome; the actual combat report determines what happened.

5. Inspect the combat report for the real chance and whether a moon formed. Reconcile debris recovery and agreed compensation. Stop or recalculate if losses or server settings differ from the plan.

title: Read events and Lifeforms separately
text:
Read events and Lifeforms separately

Official events can advertise a 40% moon chance. For example, the OGame team announced one for 1–3 September 2026 and stated that M.O.O.N. items also received the event chance. That dated announcement is evidence of the modifier, not a claim that the event is running now. Check the current server announcement before choosing a date.

The Kaelesh Supra Refractor on the planet can improve the creation chance and the size of a newly created moon. The Origin Lifeform guide gives a maximum diameter of 9,400 km. It is not a Lunar Base upgrade and does not enlarge an existing moon. The community test linked below derives roughly 8,366–8,944 km for full-base unmodified shots; this is not an official guaranteed size range.

A 2025 community test thread also documents lunar-phase effects and corrects its own initial Supra Refractor chance formula. Treat such measurements as community evidence, not an official exact formula. Use the in-game building description and the combat report when planning a modified shot.

Paid moonshots still need preparation
M.O.O.N.S. items are optional, not guaranteed moons. Read the current warm-up, resource cost and conditions. Live version 13.0.0-r14 fixed the item fleets creating debris, so do not budget a recycler return from the paid item fleet. Ordinary player-organised shots use different debris handling.

title: Reserve the field that creates the next fields
text:
Reserve the field that creates the next fields

Without bonuses a new moon begins with one available building field. Each Lunar Base level adds three fields but uses one itself: the net gain is two. Before a size limit or other modifier, total developed capacity is 1 + 3 × Lunar Base level. Used fields include every Lunar Base level and the levels of other ordinary buildings.

At Base 3, the standard capacity is 10. Base 3 + Robotics 4 + Phalanx 1 + Jump Gate 1 uses 9, leaving one for Base 4. Filling that final field with another ordinary upgrade prevents the next Base until you free space or add an applicable field bonus. Check the displayed used/total count before every upgrade.

Class fields can disappear
General adds five moon fields while active. The official class guide states that switching away removes those extra fields but does not remove existing buildings, so a moon can become overfilled. Leave room for future construction instead of treating a temporary bonus as permanent.

Lunar Base level | Total standard fields | Base itself uses | Fields left for other buildings
1 | 4 | 1 | 3
2 | 7 | 2 | 5
3 | 10 | 3 | 7
4 | 13 | 4 | 9

title: Build a small working base, then specialise
text:
Build a small working base, then specialise

As a planning example, develop Lunar Base 1, Robotics 2, Lunar Base 2, Robotics 4 and Lunar Base 3. This leaves enough standard space for Phalanx 1 and Jump Gate 1 while retaining a field for the next Base. It is a field-safe sequence, not a mandatory optimum: if construction is slow, weigh another Robotics upgrade against the Base cost and your near-term objective.

Lunar Base starts at 20,000 Metal, 40,000 Crystal and 20,000 Deuterium, doubling for each successive level. Levels 1–3 together therefore cost 140,000 / 280,000 / 140,000. Budget resources for the other buildings separately. A Jump Gate requires a second completed gate elsewhere to do useful work.

1. Build the Base and enough Robotics to make the next construction tolerable.

2. Choose whether the first useful tool is local phalanx coverage or a connection to an existing gate.

3. Add a Shipyard only when you have a specific local ship or defense requirement.

4. Recalculate free fields and construction cost before extending the plan.

title: Supply the moon as its own location
text:
Supply the moon as its own location

Moons do not have a normal mining economy, and a planet’s Nanite Factory does not accelerate its moon. Bring construction resources, scan fuel and flight fuel from elsewhere. When dispatching to the same coordinates as the planet, explicitly select the moon destination type.

Use Transport when you want the cargo delivered and the ships to return. Use Deployment when you intend ships and cargo to remain there. Check both the arrival and the resulting return event. A convenient delivery time can still produce an inconvenient cargo-fleet return.

Storage buildings are generally a poor use of scarce moon fields: imported resources can exceed the normal production storage threshold. Do not build large stores merely to receive enough resources for a gate. Keep only the stock you need for planned operations and a deliberate emergency reserve.

title: Protect the routine, not just the moon
text:
Protect the routine, not just the moon

A moon cannot itself be targeted by a Sensor Phalanx, but stationary ships can still be spied on and attacked. Moon-to-planet missions can expose information at the planet end. Learn the visibility rules in Moon tools and use the Fleetsaving guide to plan a return you can supervise.

Deathstars can destroy moons. Larger diameter makes destruction harder, but a large moon is not invulnerable. Loss of a moon can redirect relevant fleet movements to its planet, changing what an enemy can see. Avoid calling any unattended method completely safe.

Live version 12.9.0, rolled out on 26 March 2026, made Moon Destruction missions use fixed Deathstar speed 310, unaffected by higher Hyperspace Drive or server fleet-speed settings. Other Deathstar mission types retain their normal mechanics. Do not apply an old speed-universe moon-destruction timetable.

Before the first overnight save
Practise with a low-value fleet while online. Confirm origin and destination types, mission, payload, arrival or recall plan, and the time you must be present. Only scale up after you can explain what an opponent could observe at each end.

title: Price the shot after recovery, not just before it
text:
Price the shot after recovery, not just before it

A conventional player-organised Light Fighter shot spends Metal and Crystal on ships and may recover part of that value as debris. The receiving fleet or defense can also suffer losses. Add those, fuel and recycler costs before comparing two arrangements. Agreed compensation is a separate transfer governed by the community’s rules.

At 50% ship debris, 1,000 destroyed Light Fighters cost 3,000,000 Metal and 1,000,000 Crystal and create 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal of debris. If that entire field is recovered for the operation, the shot’s unrecovered ship cost is 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal, before other losses or fuel. The 2,000,000 debris meets the ordinary 20% base target.

At 80% ship debris, 625 destroyed Light Fighters cost 1,875,000 Metal plus 625,000 Crystal and create 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal of debris. Recovering the entire field leaves 375,000 Metal plus 125,000 Crystal of unrecovered ship cost, before other losses and fuel. The same 2,000,000-debris target can therefore have a different replacement bill. The raw resource totals are not a value-equivalent planning sum.

title: Distinguish the displayed chance from the debris target
text:
Distinguish the displayed chance from the debris target

A larger displayed chance can come from an event or another modifier, not only from more destroyed ships. Do not assume that a modified 20% report proves the battle generated the full 2,000,000 base-target debris. For the conventional full shot, retain the debris target as well as checking the modifier.

For an attempt that genuinely has a constant 40% success chance, three independent tries give 1 − 0.6³ =78.4% probability of at least one success. This is an illustration using a known 40% chance, not a method for calculating an event-plus-Lifeform chance. Each next attempt still has its own chance.

The public Supra Refractor guide and 2025 player tests support an effect on newly formed moon size, with 9400 km given as the maximum. The test thread corrects its initial chance equation, and the guide is marked as a draft. Keep precise stacking and rounding out of a guaranteed-cost claim unless current live evidence supports them. An existing moon does not grow merely because the planet later gains the building.

title: M.O.O.N.S. items have different debris handling
text:
M.O.O.N.S. items have different debris handling

A paid moonshot item is not equivalent to asking another player to send the same-looking fleet. The live 13.0.0-r14 notes explicitly fixed item fleets creating debris fields. Do not budget a recycler windfall from the item fleet or use its no-debris behavior to reinterpret ordinary player-organised moonshots.

Read the current item’s resource charge, delay and conditions before activating it, and prepare any defense needed for the attempt. Check the event announcement rather than assuming a past 40% event is still active. A chance-enhancing item or event is not a guarantee of a moon.

title: Choose the next moon upgrade by the job
text:
Choose the next moon upgrade by the job

A moon’s best sequence depends on the network around it. A gate on the only moon cannot yet move anything, while a modest phalanx can already answer a local question. Equally, another phalanx level may be poor value if your purpose is simply to move cargo between distant collection hubs.

Need | Useful next investment | What to check first
A first working location | Lunar Base and enough Robotics | Leave a field for the next Base.
A safe movement network | A second completed owned Jump Gate | Both moons need fuel for ordinary flights.
Information on nearby planet arrivals | Phalanx range and scan fuel | Extra range matters only if it reaches relevant systems.
Local defenses or replacement ships | Shipyard and a narrow build plan | Moon fields and construction time are limited.
A larger moon purely for durability | Evaluate another moonshot plan carefully | Replacing a developed moon sacrifices its infrastructure and still leaves risk.

title: Operating a moon network
text: Plan ready gates, local fuel and phalanx information together. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: Unlock each tool for a specific job
text:
Unlock each tool for a specific job

Build these facilities on moons, not planets. Hyperspace Technology and Hyperspace Drive are different researches: the gate prerequisite is Technology 7. Open the technology tree before transporting a large construction budget.

One gate is half a network
Budget two functioning gates if you do not already own one. An ally’s gate is not your destination. Building a gate alone does not unlock transport to another player’s moon.

Facility | Prerequisites | Level-one base cost: M / C / D | Purpose
Sensor Phalanx | Lunar Base 1 | 20,000 / 40,000 / 20,000 | Inspect eligible fleet movements at planets in range
Jump Gate | Lunar Base 1 + Hyperspace Technology 7 | 2,000,000 / 4,000,000 / 2,000,000 | Instant ship transfer between your own completed gates

title: Use a Jump Gate without stranding the fleet
text:
Use a Jump Gate without stranding the fleet

1. Confirm that the selected location is the origin moon, both gates are completed and ready, and the ships you need have actually landed there.
