2. Inspect the destination moon before jumping. Put enough Deuterium there for the next ordinary flight, plus any reserve required by your plan.

3. Open the Jump Gate, select your destination moon and enter the ships to transfer. Check the quantities rather than assuming that every ship was selected.

4. Confirm the jump, then inspect the destination fleet and the origin’s remaining ships. The transfer is instantaneous and consumes no jump fuel.

5. Check the cooldown at both endpoints. If the next step is an attack, transport or fleetsave, dispatch it separately and verify its events.

Ships travel; resources do not
A gate cannot carry your Metal, Crystal or Deuterium. Jumping cargo ships does not move the stock stored on the origin moon. Arrange resource transport separately and keep its timing in your plan.

title: Use the current cooldown, not an old wiki shortcut
text:
Use the current cooldown, not an old wiki shortcut

Both endpoints enter cooldown after a jump. Published 2025 player measurements report 60 minutes at gate level 1 in a 1 × war-fleet-speed universe and 30 minutes at 2 × . These are observations, not an official timing formula: use both gates’ displayed ready timers. Higher gate levels reduce cooldown, but it is not simply 60 minutes divided by gate level.

The live 12.0.27 release on 23 January 2025 added the maximum effective upgrade level to the technology information. The updated description quoted on the official forum states level 9. The older Buildings tutorial’s level-15 / 10-minute claim is outdated.

Player measurements published in January 2025 found approximately 53:12 at level 2, 35:44 at level 5 and 19:29 at level 9 in 1 × war speed, with no further reduction above 9. These are reported observations, not an official exact timing formula. Use the actual ready timer for operations rather than a fitted polynomial.

Plan both ends
For an A → B → C route, B has just been used even if C is ready. Do not plan the second jump immediately. Recently relocated moons can also have a separate gate lock; inspect that status before committing a fleet to the route.

title: Run a scan with a question in mind
text:
Run a scan with a question in mind

A phalanx scan costs 5,000 Deuterium at the scanning moon. Select that moon, open Galaxy, locate an eligible planet and use the phalanx action. Interface labels differ between desktop and mobile. Read the mission, endpoints and server arrival time together; the timer alone is not enough.

Decide what you are trying to learn before paying: whether a particular arrival exists, whether the fleet is outbound or returning, or whether its timing has changed. Keep a manual record of the observation time when coordinating with allies. A scan is a snapshot, not a permanent subscription to the target’s movements.

Budget the information cost
Twelve scans cost 60,000 Deuterium. If the moon begins with 70,000 and you also need 20,000 for a flight, twelve scans would leave you short. Reserve operational fuel first, then decide how many observations the situation warrants.

title: Calculate the basic coverage
text:
Calculate the basic coverage

Without class or Lifeform modifiers, range in systems to either side is L² − 1, where L is the Phalanx level. Level 1 therefore covers the moon’s own system, not zero planets. The total span on a sufficiently large non-wrapping map is 2 × range + 1 systems.

For a moon in 2:200, Phalanx 4 has base range 15 and covers systems 185 through 215 in galaxy 2, including both endpoints. It does not scan galaxy 1 or 3.

Account and universe modifiers
Discoverer has a +20% phalanx-range bonus, and Lifeform research such as Interplanetary Analysis Network can extend it. Use the displayed effective range for final eligibility; do not silently apply the unmodified table to a boosted account.

Phalanx level | Base range each side | System span including home
1 | 0 | 1
2 | 3 | 7
3 | 8 | 17
4 | 15 | 31
6 | 35 | 71

title: Ask which planet can be scanned
text:
Ask which planet can be scanned

Phalanx targets planets, not moons or debris fields. Visibility depends on the mission and the scanned endpoint. In particular, an outbound Deployment appears at its destination planet, not its origin; a recalled Deployment is absent from phalanx. Other returns to a planet can be visible at that planet.

This compact matrix describes the ordinary mission patterns. Moon destruction and redirection can change the endpoints, so reassess rather than treating the original route as permanent.

Invisible does not mean unknowable
An opponent may infer timing from earlier observations, debris disappearance or your routine. Phalanx immunity is one protection layer, not proof that a return time is secret.

Moon loss and automatic-return version caveat — Distinguish a player recall from the unverified current behavior of a same-coordinate automatic return.
https://theilluminate92.github.io/skie-guides/guide-fleetsave-reference.html#moon-loss

Movement | What a phalanx can reveal
Planet → planet, outbound Deployment | At destination planet; not at origin
Planet → moon, outbound Deployment | Neither the departure planet nor the target moon reveals that Deployment directly
Moon → planet, outbound Deployment | Visible at the destination planet
Recalled Deployment | Not visible through phalanx
Moon → planet, attack or transport | Outbound arrival can be seen at the destination planet
Moon → moon Deployment | Neither moon can be scanned directly
Moon → debris field harvesting | Neither endpoint can be scanned directly
Ordinary mission returning to a planet | Return can be visible at that planet

title: Account for the map and temporary restrictions
text:
Account for the map and temporary restrictions

When circular solar systems are enabled, phalanx coverage wraps within the same galaxy. On a 499-system circular map, systems 499 and 1 are neighbours. A level-2 base range of 3 at system 499 covers 496, 497, 498, 499, 1, 2 and 3. Circular galaxies alone do not enable this system wrap, and phalanx does not cross a galaxy boundary.

Live version 9.2.1, on 9 March 2023, prevented a moon’s phalanx from being used while combat against that moon is being calculated. A failed scan at that moment does not establish that the target fleet vanished. Check the cause before changing a timed plan.

title: Build an operating routine around the tools
text:
Build an operating routine around the tools

1. Before logging off, list every valuable fleet that will land, including cargo returning from supplying your moon network.

2. Keep a fuel reserve at the moons you expect to use. Do not depend on a gate to move resources in an emergency.

3. Check both gates’ availability and the destination’s fleet status before committing to a response. Gate mobility only helps after ships are present and the gate is ready.

4. Use moon-to-moon deployments as part of a considered fleetsave plan, with a return or recall you can supervise. Read the fleetsaving guide for the full procedure.

5. Follow current game rules. Do not use unapproved automation or attempts to obstruct another player’s phalanx or fleet controls.

A jump is not a fleetsave
If you jump to a remote moon and close the game, the ships are still stationary and attackable there. The useful question is not “Did I jump?” but “Where will my ships be while I am away, and when must I be present again?”

title: The gate timer is local to the route
text:
The gate timer is local to the route

Both endpoints participate in a jump, so a ready third gate does not make a just-used middle gate ready again. Before a planned A → B → C move, check all three displayed timers and leave enough time for B’s cooldown.

Higher gate levels can be useful for a busy network. They are much less valuable when you use a moon once a day. Compare the next level’s cost, moon field and construction time with the actual minutes it saves on the endpoint that constrains you.

The current-description quotation identifies level 9 as the effective upgrade limit. Keep old level 15 claims and fitted cooldown polynomials out of dispatch planning. War fleet speed affects gate cooldown; economy speed and expedition peaceful speed are different settings. Use the ready display for the final decision.

title: Keep a separate resource route
text:
Keep a separate resource route

A gate transfers ships without jump fuel, but it does not carry Metal, Crystal or Deuterium. Supplying a moon and moving the combat fleet are therefore two separate jobs. If the cargo ships transport resources, they also create a return flight; if they deploy, the ships remain at the destination.

Keep enough fuel at each intended operating moon for the flight that follows the jump, including a safe departure if the original plan is cancelled. A remote gate with no flight fuel can move ships into a trap rather than solve a logistics problem.

An illustrative fuel reserve starts at 120,000 Deuterium. Planned scans require 30,000 and the next launch requires 70,000, leaving 20,000. If the emergency departure you want to preserve requires 40,000, the plan is 20,000 short before any surprise occurs. Reduce scans, supply more fuel or change the route first.

title: A missing movement is a question, not a conclusion
text:
A missing movement is a question, not a conclusion

A phalanx scan is a momentary observation of eligible movements. A movement can be absent because the mission is not visible at that endpoint, a Deployment was recalled, the fleet has landed, or the scan failed. These explanations require different responses.

Read the mission and endpoint types before converting a timer into an arrival claim. Do not infer cargo from the ship count, and do not treat a fleet’s absence on one planet as proof it returned safely to a moon.

For expensive or tightly timed decisions, preserve the observation time and recheck while action is still possible. Avoid unsupported guarantees about precisely how many seconds another player needs to escape; connection delay, interface state and server processing make those claims unreliable.

title: Construction throughput and missile budgets
text: Use facilities to remove an actual bottleneck, with their side effects included. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: Unlock the capability you actually need
text:
Unlock the capability you actually need

Nanite Factories and Missile Silos are planet facilities. Build them where their effect is needed; a Nanite on one planet does not accelerate another planet or its moon. The following are standard base costs before applicable modifiers. Facility costs double with each successive level.

Capacity does not come preloaded
An empty Silo provides no interception. After unlocking ABMs, you must actually build them in the defense production menu.

Item | Requirements | Base cost: Metal / Crystal / Deuterium
Nanite Factory 1 | Robotics Factory 10 + Computer Technology 10 | 1,000,000 / 500,000 / 100,000
Missile Silo 1 | Shipyard 1 | 20,000 / 20,000 / 1,000
Anti-Ballistic Missile | Missile Silo 2 + Shipyard 1 | 8,000 / 0 / 2,000 each
Interplanetary Missile | Missile Silo 4 + Shipyard 1 + Impulse Drive 1 | 12,500 / 2,500 / 10,000 each

title: What a Nanite Factory accelerates
text:
What a Nanite Factory accelerates

Each completed Nanite level halves the standard construction time of buildings, ships and defense at that planet. Relative to Nanite 0, levels 1, 2, 3 and 4 give factors of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16. It does not directly increase mine output or speed ordinary research.

Robotics affects building construction; Shipyard affects ships and defense. Keep these roles distinct when diagnosing a slow queue. A higher Robotics level is not a substitute for Shipyard levels when producing a fleet.

Schedule a Nanite upgrade around local production. An active ship/defense queue can block the upgrade from starting, and Nanite construction blocks those production jobs. Adding an order to a queue is not the same as its being able to start. Finish needed ABMs or emergency ships before taking that production capacity offline.

Lifeform construction can also conflict with Robotics/Nanite upgrades. Check which job is actually running: adding a queue entry is not the same as starting construction.

title: Read a baseline construction calculation
text:
Read a baseline construction calculation

For an ordinary building upgrade beyond the early-level speed-up, the baseline time in hours is (Metal + Crystal cost) ÷ [2,500 × (Robotics level + 1) × 2ᴺ × economy speed], where N is the already completed Nanite level. For ships and defense, use Shipyard level in place of Robotics. Deuterium cost is not part of this timing numerator.

The example assumes no Lifeform reductions, other modifiers or acceleration items. The game applies whole-second timing and minimum durations, so doubling a very fast facility is not necessarily useful for a unit already at the minimum. Use the displayed timer for the actual purchase.

Do not apply this blindly to Lifeforms
Lifeform buildings have their own scaling and modifiers. This table explains the classic construction factor; it is not a complete formula for every Lifeform building or technology.

Example upgrade: 11,000,000 Metal + Crystal | Baseline duration | Time saved versus prior row
Robotics 10, economy × 8, Nanite 0 | 50 hours | —
Same, Nanite 1 | 25 hours | 25 hours
Same, Nanite 2 | 12 hours 30 minutes | 12 hours 30 minutes
Same, Nanite 3 | 6 hours 15 minutes | 6 hours 15 minutes

title: Buy time when time is the bottleneck
text:
Buy time when time is the bottleneck

1. List the next three construction or production jobs on the planet, their displayed durations and whether you can fund them.

2. Estimate how much of that schedule the next Nanite level saves. Include the Nanite’s own cost and the period during which its construction occupies or blocks local work.

3. Compare against the other bottleneck: if you wait days for resources and the queue is empty, faster production may not help immediately. If funded jobs are backed up, throughput has clear value.

4. Keep fuel, cargo replacement and essential defense reserves separate from the upgrade budget. Do not turn a convenience purchase into an unsafe transport situation.

5. When the upgrade completes, confirm its level and inspect the next job’s duration before filling a long queue. Record the result so that the next comparison uses your account’s actual modifiers.

A simple time comparison, not a resource-payback claim
Suppose the next funded work takes 48 hours at the current level. Halving it saves approximately 24 hours, but a Nanite upgrade occupying 30 hours would not make that short sequence finish earlier. A much longer funded backlog changes the answer. Earlier mine completion may also earn resources, which requires a separate production calculation.

title: Reserve capacity for both missile types
text:
Reserve capacity for both missile types

A Silo provides 10 capacity units per level. One ABM uses one unit and one IPM uses two: ABM count + 2 × IPM count must not exceed 10 × Silo level. Upgrading the Silo increases capacity, not missile range.

Choose a defensive reserve before filling the rest with offensive missiles. Once ABMs intercept an attack they are consumed, so remaining stock matters more than the Silo’s level. The planet’s ABMs also protect its moon against IPMs; you cannot build a separate Silo on the moon.

Do not demolish first and ask later
The archived official guide requires an empty Silo before demolition. Removing stored missiles is a separate destructive decision; upgrading the Silo is possible without emptying it. Inspect the current control and consequences before clearing anything.

Silo | Possible stock | Capacity used | What it demonstrates
2 | 20 ABMs | 20 / 20 | A small dedicated interception reserve
4 | 20 ABMs + 10 IPMs | 40 / 40 | Mixed defensive and offensive stock
5 | 10 ABMs + 20 IPMs | 50 / 50 | More offense means less interception reserve

title: Know what missiles destroy and what stops them
text:
Know what missiles destroy and what stops them

An ABM automatically destroys one incoming IPM and is itself consumed. Surviving IPMs attack defense, not the fleet or buildings. They ignore shields, and destroyed defenses do not receive the normal post-combat rebuilding chance. Attacker Weapons Technology and defender Armour Technology matter to the result.

Choose a primary defense type when launching. The aim is to remove a particular obstacle, not assume that one missile always destroys one turret. Use a current missile-capable simulator with the target’s technologies and defenses. Re-scout after impact before sending a fleet.

Interception comes before damage
If a planet has 12 ABMs and receives 20 IPMs, 12 missiles are intercepted and at most 8 reach the defenses, assuming no ABMs are added or consumed by another strike in the meantime. Those eight still need a damage calculation; “eight missiles” does not mean “eight Plasma Turrets destroyed”.

title: Separate missile range from travel time
text:
Separate missile range from travel time

The standard range is 5 × Impulse Drive level − 1 systems, within the same galaxy. Impulse 6 reaches 29 systems either way. Where circular solar systems are enabled, measure across the shorter wraparound route. Circular galaxies do not let an IPM cross into another galaxy.

The archived Formula Thread gives the baseline flight time as 30 + 60 × system distance seconds, divided by the relevant fleet-speed factor. The Origin universe-settings guide classifies missile attacks as war missions. Thus, ten systems at × 2 war speed give a baseline 315 seconds, or 5 minutes 15 seconds.

An archive inconsistency matters here
The archived IPM Guide instead prints 30 + 30 × distance. Because the official archives disagree, this guide uses the Formula Thread baseline for explanation, not a guaranteed live countdown. Verify the game’s actual flight time before synchronising missiles with a fleet.

title: Run a final check before launch
text:
Run a final check before launch

1. Confirm the exact target, including planet versus moon, and obtain a recent report of defenses, ABMs and relevant technologies.

2. Check that the missile action is available from the intended source planet. Confirm range, stock, missile count and primary target.

3. Estimate the resource cost of intercepted missiles as well as those that reach defenses. Decide whether the resulting fleet operation still has a worthwhile objective.

4. Coordinate the timing if other strikes are involved, allowing for the defender rebuilding ABMs and for changes since your last report.

5. Read the final launch details carefully. IPMs cannot be recalled after launch. After impact, inspect the report and update the plan instead of repeating a salvo automatically.

A Silo is a tool, not a safety guarantee
ABMs do not stop attacking fleets or Moon Destruction missions. Keep your defense plan proportionate and continue fleetsaving; there is no building level that replaces supervision of valuable fleet returns.

title: Include the upgrade interval in the schedule
text:
Include the upgrade interval in the schedule

The next Nanite level halves the remaining standard work you perform after it is completed; its own construction still takes time at the current level. When comparing a fixed funded backlog, let U be the upgrade duration and B the backlog’s current duration. Ignoring other interactions, upgrade-first takes U+B/2. It beats doing the backlog now only when B>2U.

If U=12 hours and B=40 hours, the upgrade-first sequence takes 32 hours and finishes 8 hours earlier. If B=16 hours, it takes 20 hours and finishes 4 hours later. This comparison values time only. Earlier mine income, future jobs, resource availability and using the upgrade to unlock something can justify a different choice.

Check Lifeform construction as well as the shipyard queue. Historical Lifeform changelog notes describe construction conflicts with Robotics/Nanite upgrades, while later interface fixes distinguish adding an entry from starting it. A queued Nanite icon is not proof that the upgrade is running. Complete urgent ABMs or cargo before starting a long local shutdown.

The cited Version 9 entries include beta and release-candidate notes, not separate proof of the current live deployment state. Check the present queue’s eligibility and technology information before scheduling conflicting work.

title: Very fast production changes the comparison
text:
Very fast production changes the comparison

Each classic Nanite level is a factor-of-two reduction before timing floors and other modifiers. Once a single unit is already at the game’s minimum displayed duration, do not assume another level doubles that unit’s practical throughput. Inspect the actual batch timer rather than extrapolating a long-job formula into the one-second range.

Choose a production test that resembles the future queue: the intended ship or defense type, realistic batch size and actual local bonuses. Another planet with different Shipyard or Lifeform facilities is not an interchangeable benchmark.

title: Pay for the missiles that interception consumes
text:
Pay for the missiles that interception consumes

Twenty IPMs cost 250,000 Metal, 50,000 Crystal and 200,000 Deuterium. Against twelve ready ABMs, twelve IPMs are intercepted and at most eight reach defenses. Your budget still spent all twenty. Count that preparation cost when deciding whether the later fleet attack is worthwhile.

A defensive stock of twelve ABMs costs 96,000 Metal and 24,000 Deuterium. That comparison explains the value of a replenished interceptor reserve, but does not mean a small silo can defeat unlimited salvos. ABMs are consumed, replacements must finish, and the same planet’s stock covers its moon.

The existing capacity and range formulas are separate:10 capacity units per Silo level, ABM 1 unit, IPM 2 units; range 5 × Impulse−1 systems in the same galaxy. The old sources disagree on missile travel-time constants. Keep the displayed live countdown authoritative rather than publishing a synchronisation promise from either archive.

title: Choose the operation before the salvo
text:
Choose the operation before the salvo

1. Identify what the missile strike is meant to remove and whether the follow-up still makes sense if the defender moves resources or adds ABMs.

2. Use a current report and include interception, technologies, target selection and the possibility of another player's simultaneous salvo.

3. Keep the planet and moon target types explicit. A planet’s ABMs can protect its moon, so a moon target does not bypass interception.

4. Check resource cost and actual stock immediately before launch. IPMs cannot be recalled after being sent.

5. Inspect the missile result and update the fleet simulation. Do not assume a fixed mixed-defense spillover order or automatic post-missile repair.

title: Compare defense by cost and outcome
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text: A reusable way to test a bunker without inventing a universal ratio. Evidence reviewed 9 November 2026. Historical formulas and unresolved live-version boundaries are labeled.

title: Make the routine raid unattractive
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Make the routine raid unattractive

Start with a practical goal: protect the production that accumulates between collections, together with vulnerable stationary assets such as satellites and crawlers. Defense is fixed to its location. A stronger bunker does not make a parked fleet or a research savings bank safe, and it cannot replace fleetsaving.

Think like a raider. Their possible return includes loot and recoverable debris; their costs include lost ships, flight fuel and any missile preparation. Your job is to make ordinary attacks unattractive at the amount you actually leave behind. Even then, someone may attack for rivalry, military destruction or amusement. Unprofitability reduces an incentive; it does not grant immunity.

Defense does not slow an incoming fleet's timer. It may make an attacker choose a different fleet or abandon the idea, but once the attack is flying, your response window comes from the mission timing. Keep movable wealth mobile, collect regularly, and preserve fuel for leaving.

Budget for the collection gap
Suppose a planet produces 200,000 resources per hour and you normally collect every eight hours. That adds 1.6 million before your next visit. Test defense against that stock plus anything already parked there, not against an empty planet. A 24-hour absence raises the production component to 4.8 million. Changing your collection routine may cost less than buying enough defense for the longer gap. These are illustrative numbers, not a recommended safe stock level.

title: Read the universe before choosing a build
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Read the universe before choosing a build

Record the separate ship-debris and defense-debris percentages. Zero defense debris does not mean zero profit: your ships, satellites, crawlers and stored resources can still be the prize. In a defense-into-debris universe, the bunker itself can contribute to the attacker's return. Do not apply the ship percentage to defenses or calculate defense debris from gross battle casualties without checking the simulator's repair treatment.

Also record whether deuterium enters debris, hostile fleet speed, fuel consumption and ACS availability. Faster hostile fleets change your response window. ACS can change the scale of fleet that reaches you. After a merge or settings change, re-run your tests instead of assuming last month's defense target remains useful.

Use opponents that actually exist nearby. A layout tested only against cargo raids tells you little about cruisers, bombers, a mixed fleet or Deathstars. Keep those scenarios separate so you can see which threat the next investment addresses.

title: Give each part of the defense a job
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Give each part of the defense a job

The cheap layer spreads random targeting across more units. Heavy guns supply stronger individual hits. That is a useful planning model, not a physical front line: an attacking shot can randomly hit a Plasma Turret even while thousands of Rocket Launchers remain. A large quantity of weak guns also cannot automatically overcome a shield threshold.

A ratio is a test candidate
Writing a layout per one Plasma Turret makes comparisons tidy. It does not make that ratio optimal. Price the whole bundle, then test equal-cost alternatives. Do not scrap existing defense just to make the counts match a prettier ratio.

Unit | Useful role | What to test
Rocket Launcher (RL) | Metal-only cheap numbers | Cruiser-heavy attacks punish an RL-heavy layout.
Light Laser (LL) | Cheap firepower and an alternative to RL | Less exposed to cruiser rapid fire, but vulnerable to destroyers.
Heavy Laser (HL) | Stronger individual shots than cheap fodder | Whether it changes losses against the small ships you face.
Ion Cannon (IC) | High shields; situational rapid fire against Reapers | Whether shield survival matters before expensive attackers destroy it.
Gauss Cannon (GC) | Heavy damage before or alongside plasma | The extra losses inflicted per resource spent.
Plasma Turret (PT) | Hard-hitting anchor; does not trigger Deathstar rapid fire | Cost, supporting fodder, bombers and missile exposure.
Small Shield Dome | One per location; useful against cargo-only raids | Its own shield must survive. It does not shield other units.
Large Shield Dome | One per location; stronger shield and possible draw against weak shots | Check actual combat bonuses. It does not guarantee protection from fighter fleets.
Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) | Intercepts IPMs rather than fighting ships | Silo capacity, remaining inventory and replacement time.

title: Understand rapid fire before adding more fodder
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Understand rapid fire before adding more fodder

Rapid fire is a chance to take another shot in the same round after hitting an eligible unit type. It is not a damage multiplier or a promise to destroy that many units. For a rapid-fire value r, the repeat chance is 1 − 1/r. At r = 10, the chance is 90%. The extra shot selects a target again; it need not hit the same unit. Destruction of the first target is not required.

The familiar examples are Cruiser versus Rocket Launcher at 10 and Destroyer versus Light Laser at 10. An Ion Cannon has rapid fire 2 against a Reaper. Mixing targets can interrupt a particular attacker's firing chains, but only if the added type is not another favorable target for that attacker. Simply adding one of everything is not an optimization.

Bombers have broad anti-defense rapid fire, including Gauss Cannons and Plasma Turrets in the post-version-7 rules. Plasma avoids Deathstar rapid fire; that does not make it immune to Deathstars or all rapid fire. Read the current in-game rapid-fire panel when testing a matchup. Very old tables predate ship additions and balance changes.

Change one thing, hold the budget steady
For a cruiser-heavy test, compare your current cheap layer with an alternative that buys more LL and fewer RL using the same resource valuation. Keep the heavy guns, research and attacker fixed. Then test both layouts against destroyers. The change that helps the first matchup can hurt the second; choose based on your threat mix, not the first favorable result.

title: Shields protect their own unit
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Shields protect their own unit

Each combat unit has its own shield and hull. A dome is another target with a large shield, not a shared force field that lends shield points to every turret. In the standard combat model, shields regenerate between rounds while hull damage persists through that battle. Surviving units finish the battle repaired; destroyed defenses are handled by the separate reconstruction step.

Small shots can bounce without reducing a strong shield. Compare one shot with the target's effective shield, rather than summing your entire fleet's attack. Older references disagree at the exact 1% boundary, and simulator authors have documented a less-than-or-equal implementation. Avoid planning a valuable fight around equality; check the current simulator and relevant live results.

Weapons, Shielding and Armour Technology change the corresponding stats. The classic technology multiplier is 1 + 0.1 × level. Structural integrity is not the combat hull number: the classic hull starts at structural integrity divided by ten. Modern class and lifeform bonuses must also be included, preferably through a current import.

Why more weak shots may not help
A shot worth 40 against an effective shield of 10,000 is only 0.4%. If the attack consists entirely of shots that bounce while that shield remains, adding more identical attackers does not chip it away. A harder-hitting unit may change the battle. This deliberately avoids the disputed exact 1% edge.

title: Count permanent losses after reconstruction
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Count permanent losses after reconstruction

Defenses destroyed in ordinary combat normally reconstruct at about 70%; the Engineer raises the normal recovery figure to about 85%. These are baseline recovery expectations, not guaranteed counts for a small batch or a substitute for checking current modifiers. The Engineer halves the expected permanent share of destroyed defense from 30% to 15% under that model. IPM destruction does not receive this reconstruction.

Losing the battle does not itself erase every defense. Count what was actually destroyed. For each type, remaining = starting − destroyed + repaired. Do not forget reconstruction or add it twice to a result that already includes it. Keep ship wreck-field recovery separate.

Repeated waves still cause attrition. Re-simulate the next wave with the post-repair remainder, not the original bunker. New construction, replenished missiles, changed fleets and different research can all invalidate a simple forecast. A draw can still be costly if the attacker loses nothing and your defenses suffer permanent losses.

Repeated total destruction: a simplified model
If every remaining unit were destroyed in each of three separate battles, with no new construction, a constant 70% recovery model leaves 1,000 × 0.7³ = 343. At 85%, it leaves about 614. Real repair rolls and partial destruction vary. The point is that recovery delays erosion; it does not make a bunker permanent.

Illustrative wave | Destroyed | Repaired | Remaining from 1,000
Normal recovery at 70% | 400 | 280 | 880
Engineer recovery at 85% | 400 | 340 | 940

title: Protect the bunker from missile preparation
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Protect the bunker from missile preparation

IPMs attack defenses independently of a fleet battle. ABMs intercept automatically at one interceptor per incoming missile, consuming both; they do not stop attacking ships. Surviving IPMs bypass shields. The attacker’s Weapons Technology and defender’s Armour Technology matter. Neither a dome nor the Engineer’s ordinary reconstruction bonus provides missile protection.

Missile Silo level 2 unlocks ABMs; level 4 unlocks IPMs with the relevant technology prerequisites. Capacity is ten slots per silo level: an ABM uses one and an IPM uses two. A moon has no missile silo, but its planet's ABMs also defend it. Keep enough capacity and resources to replenish protection rather than assuming one full silo lasts indefinitely.

After interception, the selected primary defense type is attacked. Do not rely on a guaranteed spillover order after it is exhausted. The archived tutorial describes random follow-on targets, while a later developer discussion disputes a fixed order and says the full algorithm was not published. Exact mixed-defense missile predictions deserve verification.

Count the interception budget first
A level-5 silo has 50 slots. Forty ABMs plus five IPMs use all 50. If 25 attacking IPMs arrive while those 40 ABMs are still present, the simple interception count is 25 IPMs stopped and 15 ABMs left. A later salvo faces that remainder, not the original inventory. Queued replacements are not available until completed.

title: Use missile formulas as estimates, not launch guarantees
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Use missile formulas as estimates, not launch guarantees

The classic range is 5 × Impulse Drive level − 1 systems within the same galaxy. Impulse 6 therefore gives a 29-system range. The official circular-universe announcement also allows IPM range to wrap when circular solar systems are enabled. Circular galaxies alone do not let a missile cross into another galaxy. Check actual target availability in Galaxy view. Hostile fleet speed affects missile flight time; archived guides disagree on the base expression, so use the current dispatch timing.

A classic damage estimate is surviving IPMs × 12,000 × (1 + 0.1 × attacker Weapons level). Compare that with effective defense hull, not shield points or the displayed structural integrity without conversion. This is an estimate from the older mechanics model: verify applicable modern bonuses and rounding before using it for an exact kill count.

Missiles are spent even when intercepted and cannot be recalled after launch. For a defender, the useful lesson is that armor, stocked ABMs and the ability to replenish all matter; shield upgrades alone do not solve missile exposure. A determined attacker can send repeated salvos or coordinate several launch sites.

A transparent damage estimate
Suppose five IPMs survive interception and the attacker has Weapons 10. Ignoring other bonuses, the classic damage budget is 5 × 12,000 × 2 = 120,000. If the selected defense has 20,000 effective hull per unit, that budget corresponds to six units before implementation-specific handling. Keep those assumptions visible; do not turn this illustrative example into a promise about a live target.

title: Develop defense by measured need
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Develop defense by measured need

1. Write the job: protect a particular collection interval and specified stationary assets. Set a resource ceiling that leaves room for mines, research, cargo and flight fuel.

2. Check the technology tree and purchase a small working defense rather than racing to an expensive endgame recipe. Add affordable cheap units and consider domes as they become available. Keep the early economy moving.

3. Introduce heavier guns when they change the outcome against relevant attacks. Test the next batch against the same threats and stock level used for the baseline.

4. Compare resource values consistently. If using a hypothetical 3:2:1 trade ratio, metal-equivalent cost is M + 1.5C + 3D. State the ratio and also inspect the real Crystal and Deuterium requirement; equal totals can hide a resource bottleneck.

5. Compare more units with a combat-research or defense-lifeform upgrade. An upgrade can improve existing defense, but nominal percentages alone do not show whether it crosses a useful survival or damage threshold. Include cost, completion time and the locations actually affected.

6. Prepare ABMs as defense value and local missile risk grow. After each completed batch, update the saved layout and re-test. Stop expanding when the next spend does not materially improve the protection you need.

A first defense session
On one young production planet, record the next collection time and expected stock. Inspect affordable RL/LL batches and the Small Shield Dome prerequisite in the technology tree. Compare a small cargo-only raid before and after the proposed purchase. Add a light combat escort to the attacker and test again. Build only the affordable batch that addresses your current exposure, then return to your economic goal. Repeat later with heavier threats rather than scaling the first recipe forever.

Avoid the sunk-cost trap
After an attack, rebuilding the identical bunker may recreate the identical target. First ask whether less parked wealth, a different collection interval, a safer fleet routine or a targeted composition change solves the problem more cheaply.

title: Make the simulator answer the real question
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Make the simulator answer the real question

Use a simulator maintained for the current game version, with the in-game simulator as a useful starting point. A tool being listed in an old guide is not evidence that it still works. Large-battle calculations and simulator inputs have received fixes, including live version 12.5.4 in January 2026. A PTS announcement alone does not establish behavior on your live server.

Import a recent report where possible, then inspect what arrived. Missing research or bonuses must be treated as unknown, not as zero. For a costly decision, compare several runs and plausible unfavorable inputs. Record variation in losses and draws, not just the prettiest average. A narrow simulated margin is a reason for caution.

1. Check every attacking and defending fleet, all defense counts and both domes. Include satellites, crawlers and ships that will actually be present at impact.

2. Verify Weapons, Shielding and Armour levels, player class, relevant lifeform bonuses and Engineer status. Avoid manually adding a bonus that the import already includes.

3. Check ship and defense debris percentages, deuterium-in-debris, fuel settings, coordinates and loot assumptions. The resources present at impact may exceed those on the earlier spy report.

4. Compare attacker win/draw/loss, attacker ship losses and fuel, debris they could recover, your permanent losses after reconstruction and the cost to restore production assets.

5. Run cargo raids, local fast fleets, bomber-heavy attacks and Deathstar scenarios separately. For follow-up waves, carry the post-repair result forward and account for missile preparation first.

6. Save the assumptions and compare them with real reports when available. Investigate a mismatch before committing to another large build based on the same model.

title: When an attack is already coming
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
When an attack is already coming

Confirm the destination, arrival time and what is actually exposed. Move ships and resources through a suitable fleetsave while you still can; do not wait for a new defensive batch to rescue a clearly losing position. Verify that any construction you are counting on finishes before impact.

Check the missile inventory after a salvo, not just the old espionage or build screen. Ask alliance members for help only with enough time and accurate details to coordinate. A defending fleet can change both combat and debris profitability, so it belongs in the simulation rather than being treated as free protection.

Afterward, read the report and inspect the location. Record actual repaired defense, surviving production assets, missing cargo capacity and replacement costs. Repair the operational problem first. The goal is to resume a sustainable routine without leaving the same profitable opportunity behind again.

title: Hold the budget and attacker constant
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Hold the budget and attacker constant

Make one change at a time. If you compare two cheap layers, keep the heavy guns, domes, technologies, stationary ships and resources identical. Price both alternatives in the same resource valuation. Otherwise you may simply be proving that a more expensive layout performs better.

For an equal raw-cost comparison, 1,000 Rocket Launchers cost 2,000,000 Metal, while 1,000 Light Lasers cost 1,500,000 Metal plus 500,000 Crystal. Both total 2,000,000 unweighted resource units, but they are not equal if Crystal is valued more highly. At a 2-Metal-to-1-Crystal planning valuation, the lasers cost 2,500,000 Metal-equivalent. Eight hundred lasers then match the 2,000,000 Metal-equivalent budget.

Run both candidates against a cruiser-heavy fleet, a destroyer-heavy fleet and the mixed force most plausible near you. A change that interrupts one rapid-fire chain may worsen another. Retain a choice only when its benefit matches your threat and replacement budget.

title: Test the attacker’s recovery assumptions
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Test the attacker’s recovery assumptions

Estimate what the attacker can actually take: usable loot plus debris they recover, minus fleet replacement cost, fuel and missile preparation. Use the same resource valuation on every term. A positive number in a simulator is not the same as debris safely collected.

Suppose the simplified values are 6 million loot, 4 million debris, 5 million losses and 1 million fuel. Full debris recovery gives 4 million net. Half the debris gives 2 million. No debris gives 0. If the target moves the loot as well, the operation becomes a 6-million loss under these assumptions.

This is a sensitivity test, not a prediction of enemy behaviour. Some players attack for reasons other than profit. It is still useful for deciding whether leaving extra resources or cargo behind turns an otherwise marginal attack into an attractive one.

title: Separate the first battle from restoration
page: Compare defense by cost and outcome
text:
Separate the first battle from restoration

Record both military survival and how long the economy needs to recover. A layout may preserve most defense after reconstruction but lose satellites, crawlers or cargo that kept production and collection working. Keep those replacement jobs and resources in the plan.

Use post-repair defense counts for each follow-up wave. Normal reconstruction, Engineer recovery, ship wreck fields and IPM damage are different systems. Never add an assumed repair percentage to a simulator output that already includes it.

A practical comparison records attacker losses, your permanent loss, surviving power and production assets, time to restore collection, and the amount still exposed afterward. This often gives a clearer next purchase than the win/draw label alone.

title: Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM)
text: A silo-stored interceptor for incoming Interplanetary Missiles. It does not shoot down an ordinary attacking fleet.

title: Interplanetary Missile (IPM)
text: A silo-launched weapon against defense installations. Its targeting, range and interception rules are separate from ordinary fleet combat.

title: Jump Gate
text: A moon facility that moves ships between eligible owned moons. It is not a resource transporter.

title: Lunar Base
text: A moon facility that opens building space. Keep enough free space to develop it rather than filling every available field.

title: Missile Silo
text: The planetary facility that unlocks and stores anti-ballistic and interplanetary missiles. Capacity is a stock-management constraint, not an automatic defense score.

title: Nanite Factory
text: A planetary construction-speed facility. It reduces build time but does not pay the resource cost of a build or directly speed ordinary research.

title: ACS
text: Alliance Combat System: the feature for coordinating eligible fleets in attacks or defenses. Availability and limits depend on the universe and mission.

title: Artefacts
text: Lifeform discovery rewards used to select Lifeform technologies deliberately rather than relying on random selection.

title: Astrophysics
text: Classic research that expands colony capacity and base expedition slots at specific levels. Planet-capacity and position-access requirements are separate checks.

title: Cargo
text: The resources a fleet can carry. Fuel and modifiers affect the usable space shown during dispatch.

title: Class
text: The account's selected Collector, General or Discoverer bonuses. Different from a planet's Lifeform species and from the player's chosen routine.

title: Debris field
text: Material left in space after eligible combat, collectible by the appropriate ships. Universe settings affect what becomes debris.

title: Economy speed
text: The universe multiplier for mine production and economic build speed. It also scales baseline fusion fuel use; it does not multiply energy output or replace the research and fleet-speed settings.

title: Expedition
text: A mission to position 16 with uncertain outcomes. Distinct from Lifeform discovery missions.

title: Fields
text: Available building space. Ordinary building levels occupy space; planet diameter, universe settings and applicable field effects determine the usable limit. Plan free room as well as current capacity.

title: Fleetsave
text: Sending valuable ships and resources on a carefully planned mission while you are away, timed for a return you can cover.

title: Fleet slot
text: Capacity to operate another fleet mission. Expedition limits and total fleet limits are separate constraints.

title: Holding time
text: Time a fleet spends at its expedition or holding destination, separate from outward and return travel.

title: IAS
text: Interstellar Anomaly Scanner, an Orion building. Add its eligible planet levels for total IAS; the guide separates total IAS, scan settings, observed mission rewards and historical beta13 prices.

title: Lifeforms
text: Planet-based species, buildings, population, food, and technologies. Species choice and research selection are separate decisions.

title: Payback
text: Incremental investment cost divided by additional net income over a stated period. Use consistent resource values and include required support and operating costs. Simple payback omits reinvestment and unmodeled risks.

title: Phalanx
text: Sensor Phalanx, a moon facility relevant to tracking eligible fleet movements. Fleetsaving choices must account for visibility.

title: PTS
text: Public Test Server. Mechanics and balancing seen here are not automatically the rules of a live universe.

title: Research prerequisite
text: A building or technology requirement that must be satisfied before starting the relevant research or using its unlock. IRN speed does not waive minimum-lab eligibility.

title: Resource bottleneck
text: The resource deficit that currently controls the completion time of a named goal. A large balance in another resource does not necessarily shorten that wait.

title: Tier
text: A group of Lifeform research slots with population requirements and technology selections.

title: Universe settings
text: The server-specific rules, including economy, research, fleet speeds, debris and fuel settings. Always compare like with like.

title: Research speed
text: The universe's total research-time multiplier. Use the published total once; do not multiply it by economy speed a second time.

title: Metal-equivalent
text: A planning value that converts resources using explicitly chosen weights. At 3:2:1, value is M + 1.5C + 3D. It is not the raw sum of resource units or a guaranteed exchange offer.

title: Marginal gain
text: The difference an additional purchase makes relative to the current setup, holding other assumptions consistent.

title: Mine base
text: The production amount to which a particular percentage bonus applies. It is not automatically the final hourly total including every bonus.

title: Energy
text: Power available to support production. It cannot be transported as cargo; shortages and production settings affect the income a planet can sustain.

title: Fusion Reactor
text: A durable planetary power building whose output depends on reactor level and Energy Technology and whose operation consumes Deuterium.

title: Crawler
text: A stationary production-support ship. Owned count, working-count limit, workload and realized production bonus are separate quantities.

title: Plasma Technology
text: Account-wide classic research with recurring mine-production benefits. Baseline per-level additions are 1% Metal, 0.66% Crystal and 0.33% Deuterium on the applicable mine bases.

title: Intergalactic Research Network (IRN)
text: Classic research that allows additional eligible laboratories to contribute to one normal research. A lab below that technology's own requirement does not contribute.

title: Maximum temperature (Tmax)
text: The upper temperature value used by the baseline Deuterium and satellite formulas. A slot's listed range describes possible Tmax rolls, not one planet's daily temperature cycle.
